title: What is the React Fiber architecture, and how does it enable concurrent rendering?
answer:
React Fiber is a complete rewrite of React's core reconciliation engine. It replaces the call stack reconciliation, which was synchronous and recursive, with a virtual stack frame composed of linked-list nodes called Fibers.

Each Fiber node represents a component and its state/DOM relationships. Fiber breaks rendering work into small units of work. It allows React to pause, resume, reuse, or abort rendering work based on priority using the Scheduler. This enables non-blocking UI updates, where urgent tasks like user typing can interrupt non-urgent tasks like rendering large lists.

title: Explain the two main phases of React's reconciliation process: Render Phase vs. Commit Phase.
answer:
Render Phase: React traverses the Fiber tree, calls component functions, performs reconciliation and diffing, and builds the work-in-progress tree. DOM mutations and effects are not applied during this phase. The render work can be paused, restarted, or abandoned.

Commit Phase: React applies the required DOM mutations generated during the Render Phase and runs effects and lifecycle-related work. The commit phase is synchronous and cannot be interrupted once it begins, ensuring the UI remains consistent.

title: How does React's diffing algorithm operate in O(n) time complexity instead of O(n³)?
answer:
React uses two main heuristics to reduce the complexity of tree comparison from O(n³) to approximately O(n):

  • Different element types produce different trees: If an element changes from one type to another, such as a div to a section, React replaces the old subtree instead of performing a deep comparison.
  • Stable and unique keys: Developers provide a key prop for list elements. React uses keys to identify and match children between renders, allowing it to efficiently detect insertions, deletions, and moves.

title: What happens under the hood when setState or a useState setter is called?
answer:
When a state update is triggered, React creates an update containing the new state value or updater function. The update is added to the Fiber's update queue, and React schedules the component for rendering.

During the next Render Phase, React processes the pending updates, calculates the new state, re-renders the affected components, and reconciles the resulting Fiber tree. During the Commit Phase, React applies the necessary DOM mutations.

title: Why shouldn't array indices be used as keys when rendering dynamic lists?
answer:
Using array indices as keys can break React's ability to correctly identify elements when items are inserted, deleted, or reordered.

For example, if the first item is deleted, the item that was previously at index 1 now receives key 0. React may assume that the existing element is still the same component and reuse its DOM and state. This can cause subtle bugs such as incorrect component state, lost input focus, and unexpected UI behavior.

Stable and unique identifiers from the data should be preferred as keys.

title: What is Automatic Batching in React 18+, and how does it differ from React 17?
answer:
In React 17 and earlier, React primarily batched state updates inside React event handlers. Updates triggered inside promises, setTimeout, or native event handlers could cause separate renders.

React 18 introduced Automatic Batching, which groups multiple state updates into a single render even when the updates occur inside promises, timers, native event handlers, or other asynchronous contexts.

When synchronous DOM updates are required immediately, React provides flushSync to opt out of normal batching behavior.

title: Compare useEffect and useLayoutEffect. When would you choose useLayoutEffect?
answer:
useEffect runs after React has committed the DOM and generally after the browser has painted. It is suitable for non-visual side effects such as data fetching, subscriptions, logging, and synchronization with external systems.

useLayoutEffect runs synchronously after DOM mutations but before the browser paints. Because it can block painting, it should be used carefully.

Use useLayoutEffect when you need to measure DOM elements or make DOM changes before the user sees the result, such as positioning a tooltip or popover and preventing visual flickering.

title: What is useInsertionEffect and when should it be used?
answer:
useInsertionEffect is a React hook introduced in React 18. It runs before DOM mutations and before useLayoutEffect.

Its primary purpose is to allow CSS-in-JS libraries to inject styles before layout effects and browser layout calculations occur. This helps prevent unnecessary layout recalculations and visual inconsistencies.

Application developers generally should not use useInsertionEffect directly. It is mainly intended for library authors, particularly CSS-in-JS library implementations.

title: What is the execution order of useEffect in parent and child components during mounting and updating?
answer:
During mounting, React renders the parent and its children first. After the commit, passive effects created with useEffect are executed. In common cases, child effects run before parent effects.

During unmounting, cleanup functions are executed as React removes components from the tree. The cleanup ordering can differ from mount effect ordering, so application code should not rely on a simplistic parent-first or child-first rule for every effect scenario.

The important distinction is that rendering happens before effects, and useEffect runs after the commit rather than during rendering.

title: Explain the purpose of useTransition and how it differs from useDeferredValue.
answer:
Both APIs deprioritize non-urgent updates to keep the UI responsive.

  • useTransition: Provides a startTransition function that lets you mark state updates as non-urgent. It also provides an isPending state indicator. It is useful for operations such as filtering a large dataset.
  • useDeferredValue: Accepts a value, such as a search query, and returns a deferred version of that value. The deferred value can temporarily lag behind the current value while React finishes urgent updates.

The key difference is that useTransition is used to mark state updates as non-urgent, while useDeferredValue is used to defer the value itself.

title: How do React Server Components (RSC) differ from Server-Side Rendering (SSR)?
answer:
SSR: Server-Side Rendering runs components on the server to generate HTML that is sent to the browser. The client then downloads the required JavaScript and hydrates the application. Interactive components, state, and event handlers still execute on the client.

RSC: React Server Components execute only on the server and do not ship their component JavaScript to the client. They produce a serialized React Server Components payload that the client uses to construct the UI. Server Components cannot use client-side state, effects, or DOM event handlers.

RSCs can also access server-side resources such as databases directly, which can reduce the need for additional API layers for some use cases.

title: Explain the double-render behavior in React 18 Strict Mode during development.
answer:
In React 18 development mode, Strict Mode intentionally performs an additional mount and unmount cycle for components to help identify side effects that are not resilient to being mounted and cleaned up correctly.

For effects, React may run the setup, cleanup, and setup sequence again during development. This helps developers discover problems such as uncleaned timers, subscriptions, event listeners, or WebSocket connections.

This behavior is development-only and does not mean that production applications render components twice. It also helps prepare components for React's concurrent rendering capabilities.

title: What is a stale closure in custom hooks, and how do you resolve it?
answer:
A stale closure occurs when an asynchronous function, callback, or effect captures a variable from an earlier render and continues using that outdated value.

Common ways to resolve stale closures include:

  • Provide accurate dependency arrays to hooks such as useEffect and useCallback.
  • Use functional state updates, such as setCount(prev => prev + 1), when the new state depends on the previous state.
  • Use useRef when you need to store a mutable value across renders without triggering a re-render.

title: Contrast Context API vs. Redux Toolkit / Zustand for enterprise state management.
answer:
Context API: Context is useful for relatively low-frequency global values such as themes, locale settings, or authentication information. When the provided Context value changes, consumers that read that context can re-render, which can become inefficient for frequently changing state.

Redux Toolkit / Zustand: These are external state-management solutions that maintain state outside the React component tree. They provide mechanisms such as selectors, middleware, and developer tools. With appropriate selectors, components can subscribe to specific parts of the state and avoid unnecessary re-renders.

For enterprise applications, the choice depends on requirements such as state complexity, debugging needs, team conventions, middleware requirements, and update frequency.

title: What are the common performance metrics to optimize in a large-scale React app?
answer:
Common web performance metrics include:

  • FCP (First Contentful Paint): Measures how quickly the first meaningful content is displayed. Techniques such as fast HTML delivery and code splitting can help.
  • LCP (Largest Contentful Paint): Measures how quickly the largest visible content element is rendered. Image optimization, critical resource optimization, and server-side rendering can improve LCP.
  • INP (Interaction to Next Paint): Measures interaction responsiveness. Reducing long main-thread tasks, optimizing expensive renders, and using techniques such as transitions or Web Workers can help.
  • CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift): Measures unexpected layout movement. Reserving dimensions for images and asynchronous content helps maintain layout stability.

title: How do you implement fine-grained code splitting in React?
answer:
Fine-grained code splitting can be implemented by combining dynamic import() with React.lazy() and Suspense.

Route-based code splitting creates separate JavaScript chunks for different routes. Feature-based code splitting can defer heavy components, such as chart libraries, editors, or modal dialogs, until they are actually needed.

const HeavyChart = React.lazy(() => import('./HeavyChart'));

function Dashboard() {
  return (
    <Suspense fallback={<div>Loading...</div>}>
      <HeavyChart />
    </Suspense>
  );
}

title: How does React handle synthetic events, and how did event delegation change in React 17?
answer:
React uses SyntheticEvent, a cross-browser wrapper around native browser events that provides a consistent event interface.

  • React 16 and earlier: React primarily delegated events to the document object.
  • React 17+: React changed event delegation so that events are attached to the root DOM container where the React tree is rendered.

This change makes it easier to embed multiple React versions or integrate multiple React applications and micro-frontends on the same page without the event handling behavior of one application interfering with another.

title: What is component hydration, and what causes Hydration Mismatch errors?
answer:
Hydration is the process where React attaches behavior, event handlers, and client-side logic to HTML that was already generated on the server.

A Hydration Mismatch occurs when the HTML generated by the server differs from the output React expects during the client's initial render.

Common causes include using browser-only APIs such as window.innerWidth during rendering, generating dynamic values such as new Date(), using random values, or having invalid HTML nesting.

The server and client's initial render should produce matching markup before client-only behavior is applied.

title: Explain the use case of useSyncExternalStore.
answer:
useSyncExternalStore is a React hook designed for subscribing to external stores safely, particularly in concurrent rendering environments.

It is commonly used by state-management and library authors to integrate external data sources such as Redux stores, browser APIs, or other subscription-based stores with React.

The hook helps React maintain a consistent view of external state during concurrent rendering and prevents problems such as tearing, where different components could otherwise observe inconsistent versions of the same external state.

title: How would you design a custom hook to cancel pending API requests on component unmount or search query change?
answer:
You can use AbortController inside a useEffect. A new controller is created whenever the URL changes, and the cleanup function aborts the previous request when the component unmounts or before the effect runs again.

function useFetch(url: string) {
  const [data, setData] = useState(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    const controller = new AbortController();

    fetch(url, { signal: controller.signal })
      .then(res => res.json())
      .then(setData)
      .catch(err => {
        if (err.name !== 'AbortError') {
          console.error(err);
        }
      });

    return () => controller.abort();
  }, [url]);

  return data;
}

This prevents obsolete requests from updating state after the component has unmounted or after the search query has changed.

title: What is the Render Props pattern, and how does it compare to Custom Hooks?
answer:
The Render Props pattern passes a function as a prop to a component. The component calls that function and provides it with state or behavior, allowing the consumer to control how the UI is rendered.

Modern React has largely replaced Render Props with Custom Hooks because custom hooks allow developers to reuse stateful logic without adding extra wrapper components. This reduces component nesting and keeps component trees easier to read and maintain.

title: Describe Higher-Order Components (HOCs) and their drawbacks.
answer:
A Higher-Order Component (HOC) is a function that accepts a component and returns a new enhanced component.

const EnhancedComponent = withAuth(MyComponent);

Common drawbacks include prop collisions, hidden dependencies, complex TypeScript typings, and additional wrapper components that can make the component tree harder to understand. Custom Hooks are generally preferred for sharing stateful logic in modern React applications, although HOCs can still be useful in some scenarios and legacy class-component architectures.

title: How do React Portals work, and how does event bubbling behave through them?
answer:
React Portals allow a component's children to be rendered into a DOM node outside the normal DOM hierarchy of the parent component.

createPortal(child, container);

Although the portal content is physically rendered elsewhere in the DOM, it remains part of the same React tree. Therefore, events triggered inside a portal can bubble through the React component tree to React ancestors, even though those elements are not DOM ancestors.

Portals are commonly used for modals, dialogs, tooltips, dropdowns, and other UI elements that need to escape CSS overflow or stacking contexts.

title: What are Error Boundaries? Why can't functional components implement them directly?
answer:
Error Boundaries are React components that catch JavaScript errors in their child component tree, log those errors, and display a fallback UI instead of allowing the entire application UI to crash.

Traditionally, Error Boundaries are implemented using class components with lifecycle methods such as getDerivedStateFromError and componentDidCatch.

React does not currently provide a Hook equivalent for these specific Error Boundary lifecycle capabilities. Functional components can be used inside an Error Boundary, but the boundary itself still requires the supported Error Boundary mechanism.

title: Explain the Compound Components pattern with an example.
answer:
The Compound Components pattern allows multiple related components to share state implicitly while giving consumers flexible control over the structure and layout of the UI.

A common example is an Accordion with components such as Accordion and Accordion.Item. The parent component can store shared state in Context, while child components consume that state using useContext.

const AccordionContext = createContext(null);

function Accordion({ children }) {
  const [openIndex, setOpenIndex] = useState(null);

  return (
    <AccordionContext.Provider value={{ openIndex, setOpenIndex }}>
      {children}
    </AccordionContext.Provider>
  );
}

Accordion.Item = function Item({ index, children }) {
  const { openIndex, setOpenIndex } = useContext(AccordionContext);

  return (
    <div onClick={() => setOpenIndex(index)}>
      {openIndex === index && children}
    </div>
  );
};

This pattern produces an expressive API such as <Accordion><Accordion.Item /></Accordion> while keeping the shared state inside the component group.

title: What is the Control Props pattern?
answer:
The Control Props pattern allows a component to support both controlled and uncontrolled usage.

In uncontrolled mode, the component manages its own internal state. In controlled mode, the parent component provides the current value and controls state changes through explicit props and callbacks.

This pattern gives consumers flexibility: they can use a component with simple internal state or take complete control of its state when more advanced behavior is required.

title: How do uncontrolled components differ from controlled components? When would you use uncontrolled?
answer:
Controlled components have their state managed by React. For example, an input receives a value prop and updates that value through an onChange handler. They are useful for real-time validation, formatted inputs, conditional UI, and dynamically enabling or disabling submission.

Uncontrolled components allow the DOM to maintain the current value. React can access the value using a ref, such as useRef.

Uncontrolled components can be useful for simpler forms, file inputs such as <input type="file" />, and integrations with non-React or legacy DOM code. They can also reduce the number of React state updates in large forms, although controlled forms are often preferred when the application needs to react to every input change.

title: How do you implement micro-frontends with React?
answer:
Micro-frontends decompose a large frontend application into smaller, independently developed and deployed applications or features.

With React, common approaches include Webpack Module Federation and frameworks such as single-spa. A host application can dynamically load remote React modules or bundles at runtime.

Shared dependencies such as react and react-dom can be configured as shared singletons to avoid loading multiple copies of the React runtime.

Micro-frontends can provide team autonomy and independent deployments, but they also introduce additional complexity around routing, shared state, communication, dependency management, performance, and consistent user experience.

title: What is the difference between React.memo, useMemo, and useCallback?
answer:
• React.memo: A higher-order component that memoizes a component and allows React to skip rendering it when its props have not changed according to the configured comparison.
  • useMemo: Memoizes the result of a calculation between renders. It is useful when a calculation is expensive and its dependencies have not changed.
  • useCallback: Memoizes a function reference between renders. It is useful when passing callbacks to memoized child components or when a stable function identity is required.

These APIs should be used based on actual rendering or calculation costs rather than automatically applying memoization everywhere, because memoization itself has overhead.

title: Explain memory leak scenarios in React apps and how to detect and fix them.
answer:
Common sources of resource leaks in React applications include uncleared setInterval or setTimeout timers, uncancelled network requests, event listeners that are not removed, and active RxJS or WebSocket subscriptions that continue after a component is unmounted.

You can investigate memory problems using browser developer tools such as the Chrome DevTools Memory panel, heap snapshots, allocation profiling, and inspection of retained or detached DOM nodes.

The typical solution is to clean up resources in the cleanup function returned by useEffect.

useEffect(() => {
  const timer = setInterval(doSomething, 1000);

  return () => {
    clearInterval(timer);
  };
}, []);

title: How do you unit test custom hooks using React Testing Library?
answer:
React Testing Library provides renderHook for rendering and testing custom hooks. The act utility is used when triggering state updates so React can process the updates before assertions are made.

import { renderHook, act } from '@testing-library/react';

test('should increment counter', () => {
  const { result } = renderHook(() => useCounter());

  act(() => {
    result.current.increment();
  });

  expect(result.current.count).toBe(1);
});

This approach tests the hook's observable behavior without requiring a separate component solely for testing the hook.

title: What is the core philosophy of React Testing Library vs. Enzyme?
answer:
Enzyme historically focused more on implementation details, such as component state, internal methods, component instances, and shallow rendering.

React Testing Library promotes user-centric testing. Instead of testing how a component is implemented internally, tests interact with the rendered UI using queries based on things users can perceive, such as accessible roles, labels, text, and other DOM behavior.

This approach generally produces tests that are more resilient to internal refactoring because they focus on observable behavior rather than implementation details.

title: What is the purpose of act() in React testing?
answer:
act() ensures that React updates triggered by a test action are processed before assertions are made. This includes state updates, effects, and DOM changes associated with the tested interaction.

Wrapping interactions or state-changing operations in act() helps tests accurately reflect what the user would observe after React has finished processing the update.

act(() => {
  result.current.increment();
});

expect(result.current.count).toBe(1);

React Testing Library's higher-level utilities often wrap updates in act() automatically, so you usually only need to call it directly when testing lower-level or custom update mechanisms.

title: What is the difference between useImperativeHandle and standard ref forwarding (forwardRef)?
answer:
forwardRef allows a parent component to pass a ref through a child component to an underlying DOM element or another component.

useImperativeHandle allows the child component to customize what is exposed through that ref. Instead of exposing the entire DOM node, the child can expose only specific imperative methods such as focus() or reset().

This provides better encapsulation because the parent does not need direct access to the child's internal DOM structure.

title: How does React Fiber handle priority levels?
answer:
Modern React uses a Lane-based priority system to represent and schedule updates. Different updates can be assigned different lanes depending on their urgency.

For example, urgent user interactions can receive higher-priority lanes, while less urgent background updates can use lower-priority lanes. React can then process higher-priority work first and defer lower-priority work when necessary.

This scheduling model allows React to keep the UI responsive while managing multiple updates and concurrent rendering work.

title: Why shouldn't you call Hooks inside loops, conditions, or nested functions?
answer:
React relies on the order in which Hooks are called to associate each Hook with its internal state and Fiber data.

If a Hook is called conditionally, inside a loop, or from a nested function, the number or order of Hook calls can change between renders. This can cause React to associate state and effects with the wrong Hook.

Therefore, Hooks must be called at the top level of React function components or custom Hooks, following the Rules of Hooks.

title: What are CSS-in-JS performance bottlenecks in React, and how does Zero-Runtime CSS solve them?
answer:
Runtime CSS-in-JS solutions can generate and inject styles during application execution. When styles depend on frequently changing props, this can introduce additional JavaScript work and CSS recalculation, especially when rendering large lists.

Zero-Runtime CSS moves most style generation to build time. Tools such as Linaria and vanilla-extract can extract styles into static CSS files, while utility-based approaches such as Tailwind CSS can also minimize runtime styling work.

This reduces JavaScript overhead during rendering because the browser can load and apply pre-generated CSS rather than requiring React-related JavaScript to generate styles at runtime.

title: How do you implement virtualization for long lists in React?
answer:
Virtualization renders only the items currently visible in the viewport, plus a small buffer, instead of rendering every item in a large dataset.

Libraries such as react-window can calculate which items should be rendered based on the current scroll position. Items are positioned appropriately so the user experiences the list as if all items were present.

This keeps the number of active DOM nodes closer to the number of visible items rather than the total number of items, significantly improving rendering, memory usage, and scrolling performance for large lists.

title: What is React Compiler (React Forget)?
answer:
React Compiler, previously associated with the codename React Forget, is a compiler developed by the React team that can automatically optimize React code through memoization.

It analyzes component code and React semantics at build time and can insert appropriate memoization so that components, calculations, and values do not need to be manually optimized in every situation.

The goal is to reduce the need for developers to manually add useMemo, useCallback, and React.memo solely for performance optimization.

title: Describe the Server Action concept in modern React frameworks.
answer:
Server Actions are asynchronous server-side functions that can be invoked from application UI code, particularly in frameworks that integrate React Server Components and server-side mutations.

For example, a Server Action can be connected to a form's action and execute database or other server-side operations without requiring the developer to manually create a separate REST endpoint for that operation.

They provide a convenient mechanism for handling server-side mutations while maintaining a clear boundary between client and server execution.

title: How does React prevent XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) vulnerabilities by default?
answer:
React automatically escapes string values inserted into JSX expressions. For example, if user-controlled content is rendered using {'{userInput}'}, React treats the value as text rather than interpreting it as HTML.

This prevents malicious HTML and script content from being directly interpreted by the browser in normal JSX rendering.

However, APIs such as dangerouslySetInnerHTML intentionally bypass React's normal escaping and therefore require careful handling of untrusted content.

title: How do you safely render raw HTML in React while mitigating XSS?
answer:
When raw HTML must be rendered, the HTML should be sanitized before passing it to dangerouslySetInnerHTML. A commonly used library for this purpose is DOMPurify.

import DOMPurify from 'dompurify';

function SafeHtml({ htmlString }: { htmlString: string }) {
  const cleanHtml = DOMPurify.sanitize(htmlString);

  return <div dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: cleanHtml }} />;
}

Sanitization removes or neutralizes potentially dangerous markup and attributes before the HTML is inserted into the DOM. You should also avoid bypassing sanitization with untrusted content.

title: What is tree-shaking, and how do you ensure your React components are tree-shakeable?
answer:
Tree-shaking is a build-time optimization that uses static analysis of ES Modules to identify and eliminate unused code from the final JavaScript bundle.

To make code more tree-shakeable:

  • Prefer ES Module import/export syntax.
  • Use named exports where appropriate instead of exporting large objects containing unrelated functionality.
  • Avoid unnecessary side-effect imports.
  • Mark packages with "sideEffects": false in package.json when that declaration is correct for the package.
  • Use build tools such as Vite, Rollup, or modern webpack configurations that support tree-shaking.

title: What is strict equality check in React state updates, and why does mutating state fail to trigger re-renders?
answer:
React uses Object.is() semantics when determining whether a state value has changed.

If an object or array is mutated directly, its reference remains the same. For example, calling state.push(1) changes the existing array but does not create a new reference. React may therefore consider the state unchanged because Object.is(oldState, newState) is true.

Instead, create a new object or array when updating state.

setItems(prev => [...prev, newItem]);

Immutable updates make the state change detectable and allow React to schedule the appropriate re-render.

title: Explain how React Suspense works under the hood.
answer:
When a component cannot complete rendering because it is waiting for something, such as a lazy-loaded component or supported asynchronous data, React can suspend that part of the tree.

Conceptually, the suspended work signals to React that the component is not ready to complete rendering. The nearest Suspense boundary can then render its fallback UI while React waits for the suspended work to become available.

Once the required resource is ready, React schedules another render attempt and can replace the fallback with the resolved content.

<Suspense fallback={<Loading />}>
  <LazyComponent />
</Suspense>

title: What is the purpose of useActionState (formerly useFormState)?
answer:
useActionState is a React Hook designed to manage the state produced by an action, particularly useful for form submissions and asynchronous mutations.

It accepts an action function and an initial state and returns the current state, a function that can be used to invoke the action, and a pending indicator.

This makes it easier to represent submission results such as validation errors, success messages, or other server-generated state while also tracking whether the action is pending.

title: How do you avoid context re-render cascades for complex objects?
answer:
There are several strategies for reducing unnecessary re-renders caused by Context updates:

  • Split large contexts: Use smaller, focused contexts such as UserContext and ThemeContext instead of putting unrelated state into one context.
  • Memoize provider values: Use useMemo when appropriate so the Context value object does not receive a new reference on every parent render.
  • Optimize consumers: Use component boundaries and memoization where appropriate to prevent unrelated work.
  • Use external stores for complex high-frequency state: State-management libraries can provide selectors that allow components to subscribe to specific state slices.

title: Explain the difference between ref.current mutation vs state mutation.
answer:
Updating ref.current mutates a value stored in a ref without scheduling a React re-render. The value persists between renders and can be read or changed synchronously.

Updating React state through its setter schedules React to process a state update and potentially re-render the component.

Use refs for mutable values that do not need to drive the UI, such as DOM references, timer IDs, or previous values. Use state when a value affects what should be rendered.

title: How do you implement a dynamic theme switcher without causing UI flicker on initial page load?
answer:
To prevent theme flickering, determine the user's preferred theme before the initial application render and browser paint.

A common approach is to execute a small inline script in the HTML document before the main React bundle loads. The script checks a stored theme preference or the prefers-color-scheme media query and synchronously applies a class or data attribute to the document element.

const theme = localStorage.getItem('theme') ||
  (window.matchMedia('(prefers-color-scheme: dark)').matches ? 'dark' : 'light');

document.documentElement.classList.add(theme);

Because the correct theme is applied before the initial layout is painted, the user avoids seeing the default theme briefly before React switches to the preferred theme.

title: How would you handle continuous high-frequency events like window resizing or mouse moves in React?
answer:
High-frequency events such as resize, scroll, and mousemove can trigger excessive JavaScript execution and React renders.

Common optimization techniques include:

  • Throttling: Limit how frequently the handler executes.
  • Debouncing: Wait until events stop occurring for a specified period before executing the handler.
  • useRef: Store mutable values or timer IDs without triggering re-renders.
  • useCallback: Maintain a stable handler reference when necessary.
  • requestAnimationFrame: Coordinate visual updates with the browser's rendering cycle.
  • Direct DOM updates: For specific animation or measurement scenarios, refs can be used to avoid unnecessary React renders.

The appropriate technique depends on whether the application needs continuous updates, updates after the event settles, or animation-synchronized updates.

title: How does GraphQL differ structurally and architecturally from REST?
answer:
REST is a resource-centric architectural style where different resources are typically exposed through separate endpoints, such as /api/users/1. Clients may receive more data than they need (over-fetching) or need multiple requests to obtain related data (under-fetching).

GraphQL typically exposes a single endpoint such as /graphql. Clients declare the exact shape of the data they need using GraphQL's query language. The server uses a strongly typed schema and resolver system to dynamically compose the requested data.

title: Explain the execution cycle of a GraphQL query on the server.
answer:
A GraphQL query generally goes through three major stages:

  1. Parsing: The server parses the incoming GraphQL query string into an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST).
  2. Validation: The AST is validated against the GraphQL schema. This includes checking types, fields, arguments, directives, and other schema rules.
  3. Execution: The server executes the requested root fields and invokes their resolver functions. Resolvers then resolve nested fields according to the query selection set and produce a response matching the requested GraphQL shape.

title: What are scalar, object, interface, union, and input types in GraphQL SDL?
answer:
• Scalar: Represents primitive leaf values such as String, Int, Float, Boolean, and ID. Custom scalars such as DateTime can also be defined.
  • Object: Represents a concrete GraphQL type containing one or more fields.
  • Interface: Defines a common set of fields that implementing object types must provide.
  • Union: Represents a type that can resolve to one of several object types without requiring those types to share the same fields.
  • Input: Defines structured objects that can be passed as arguments to queries or mutations.

title: How do Interfaces and Unions differ, and how are fragment type conditions (... on Type) used?
answer:
Interfaces define a common set of fields that implementing object types must provide. This allows clients to query those shared fields directly.

Unions represent a set of possible object types without requiring those types to share a common field contract.

When querying type-specific fields from an interface or union, clients can use inline fragments with type conditions such as ... on User or ... on Post.

query GetSearchResults {
  search(query: "react") {
    ... on User {
      username
    }
    ... on Post {
      title
    }
  }
}

title: What are GraphQL Directives? Contrast @include, @skip, and custom directives.
answer:
GraphQL directives provide metadata or instructions that can modify how fields, fragments, or schema definitions are handled.

  • @include(if: Boolean): Includes a field or fragment only when the provided condition is true.
  • @skip(if: Boolean): Skips a field or fragment when the provided condition is true.
  • Custom directives: Application-specific directives can be implemented for concerns such as authorization, caching, validation, formatting, or other server-side behavior.

For example, a server may define a custom directive such as @auth(role: ADMIN) to enforce authorization rules.

title: What is Schema First vs Code First schema design?
answer:
Schema First starts by defining the GraphQL schema using SDL files. Developers then generate or manually create language types and implement resolver functions that conform to the schema.

Code First starts with programming-language constructs such as classes, decorators, or builder APIs. Libraries such as TypeGraphQL, Nexus, or NestJS can generate the GraphQL schema from the application code.

Schema First emphasizes an explicit API contract, while Code First can provide stronger integration with the application's programming language and type system.

title: How do you handle file uploads in GraphQL?
answer:
GraphQL itself is designed around structured request data and does not define native binary file-upload semantics.

Common approaches include:

  • GraphQL Multipart Request Specification: A multipart HTTP request can be used with server implementations that support file uploads.
  • Pre-signed cloud storage URLs: The GraphQL mutation generates a short-lived upload URL. The client then uploads the binary file directly to cloud storage such as Amazon S3 using HTTP.

For large files and scalable systems, direct uploads to object storage using pre-signed URLs are often preferred because they avoid sending large binary payloads through the GraphQL server.

title: How is pagination best handled in GraphQL? Compare Offset vs Cursor-based pagination.
answer:
Offset/Limit pagination uses parameters such as offset and limit. It is simple to implement, but large offsets can become inefficient depending on the database and query plan. It can also produce skipped or duplicated items when records are inserted or deleted while a user is paging through results.

Cursor-based pagination uses an opaque cursor representing a position in the result set. The Relay-style Connection pattern commonly uses fields such as first, after, edges, node, and pageInfo.

query GetPosts {
  posts(first: 10, after: "cursor_xyz") {
    edges {
      cursor
      node {
        id
        title
      }
    }
    pageInfo {
      hasNextPage
      endCursor
    }
  }
}

Cursor-based pagination is generally better suited to large, changing datasets where stable pagination is important.

title: What is the N+1 Query Problem in GraphQL, and how is it solved?
answer:
The N+1 query problem occurs when a GraphQL query first performs one database query to retrieve N parent records and then performs an additional database query for each parent's related data.

For example, fetching 100 users could result in one query for the users and another 100 queries for their posts.

A common solution is DataLoader. It batches multiple requests for related entities into a single database query, such as SELECT * FROM children WHERE parent_id IN (...), and can cache results for the duration of the request.

title: How does DataLoader's batching and caching mechanism work under the hood?
answer:
DataLoader collects multiple load(key) calls that occur within the same batching window and combines them into a single batch operation.

As GraphQL resolvers request related data, each resolver can call dataLoader.load(key). DataLoader collects the requested keys and then invokes the batch-loading function with those keys. The batch function can perform one database query and return the results corresponding to each requested key.

DataLoader also provides request-scoped memoization by default. This means repeated requests for the same key during a request can reuse the previously loaded result rather than querying the database again.

title: Compare Client-side Normalized Caching vs Document Caching.
answer:
Document caching stores the complete response for a particular GraphQL operation, often using the query and variables as part of the cache key. It is relatively simple but can duplicate the same entity data across multiple cached query results.

Normalized caching, used by clients such as Apollo Client and URQL, decomposes nested responses into individual entities and stores them using identifiers such as __typename:id.

With normalized caching, when an entity is updated, multiple queries or UI components that reference that entity can observe the updated data without requiring each complete query result to be independently replaced.

title: What are Persisted Queries (APQ), and what problems do they solve?
answer:
Automatic Persisted Queries (APQ) reduce the amount of GraphQL query text that needs to be transmitted over the network.

  1. The client calculates a hash, commonly using SHA-256, for the GraphQL query.
  2. The client initially sends the hash to the server.
  3. If the server already knows the hash, it retrieves the corresponding query and executes it.
  4. If the hash is unknown, the client can send the complete query so the server can register it.

This can significantly reduce request payload sizes and, depending on the server and infrastructure, can enable GraphQL operations to use HTTP GET requests that are more compatible with standard HTTP and CDN caching.

title: How do HTTP Caching and CDN integration work with GraphQL?
answer:
GraphQL commonly uses a single endpoint and POST requests, which makes traditional HTTP caching less straightforward than resource-oriented REST APIs.

One approach is to use Persisted Queries and expose operations through HTTP GET requests where appropriate. GET requests can then be cached by compatible CDNs and HTTP caches.

GraphQL servers can also provide caching metadata such as Cache-Control headers. Some GraphQL implementations allow cache hints or directives to define different cache policies for fields and types.

title: What is GraphQL Query Cost Analysis (Complexity Limiting)?
answer:
Query complexity analysis assigns a cost to fields or operations and calculates the estimated cost of a GraphQL query before execution.

This helps protect the server from expensive or intentionally abusive queries, such as deeply nested relationships or large list fields. A query can be rejected during validation if its calculated complexity exceeds a configured threshold.

Complexity rules can also apply multipliers to list fields so that requesting a large number of records produces a proportionally higher estimated cost.

title: How do you implement Query Depth Limiting?
answer:
Query depth limiting analyzes the GraphQL query AST before execution and calculates how deeply fields are nested.

A maximum depth can be configured, such as six levels. If a query exceeds the configured limit, the server rejects it before executing expensive resolver operations.

Depth limiting is useful as a defensive measure against deeply nested queries, but it is often combined with query complexity analysis because a shallow query containing very expensive list fields can still consume significant server resources.

title: Explain Apollo Federation architecture (Supergraph vs Subgraphs).
answer:
Apollo Federation combines independently owned GraphQL services into a single unified supergraph.

  • Subgraphs: Independent domain services such as Users, Products, and Orders. Each subgraph owns and defines the schema for its domain.
  • Router: The entry point for clients. It receives GraphQL operations, creates a query plan based on the supergraph schema, delegates field-level work to the appropriate subgraphs, and combines their results into a single response.

This architecture allows teams to develop and deploy domain-specific GraphQL services independently while clients interact with one unified API.

title: How do entities and @key directives work in Apollo Federation?
answer:
Entities are types that can be referenced or extended across multiple Federation subgraphs. The @key directive identifies the fields that uniquely identify an entity.

For example, a Products subgraph can define a Product entity using its ID:

type Product @key(fields: "id") {
  id: ID!
  name: String!
}

Another subgraph can extend that entity and contribute additional fields:

extend type Product @key(fields: "id") {
  id: ID! @external
  reviews: [Review]
}

The router can use the entity key to retrieve additional fields from the appropriate subgraph.

title: What is the difference between Schema Stitching and Apollo Federation?
answer:
Schema Stitching is an approach where a gateway combines multiple GraphQL schemas programmatically. The gateway can manually configure schema transformations and resolvers to connect related types and fields from different services.

Apollo Federation uses a declarative federation specification. Subgraphs define ownership, relationships, and entity keys using GraphQL directives. The federation router uses this metadata to build a unified supergraph and automatically plan how client queries should be distributed across subgraphs.

In short, Schema Stitching traditionally relies more on gateway-side composition and custom glue code, while Federation moves much of the composition model into the subgraph schemas.

title: How do you implement Authorization in GraphQL (Field-Level vs Middleware)?
answer:
Field-Level Authorization: Authorization checks can be performed inside resolvers or, preferably, within domain/business services. The logic verifies the authenticated user's identity, roles, permissions, or ownership before returning protected data.

Schema Directive / Middleware: Authorization rules can also be expressed declaratively using schema directives or middleware. For example, a custom directive such as @auth(requires: ADMIN) can enforce access rules before a resolver executes.

Business-critical authorization should remain enforced in the domain/service layer so that it cannot be bypassed simply by accessing the same business operation through another API path.

title: How do you secure a public GraphQL API against denial-of-service (DoS) attacks?
answer:
A public GraphQL API should apply multiple layers of protection against expensive or malicious queries:

  • Query Depth Limiting: Restrict excessively nested queries.
  • Query Complexity Analysis: Reject queries whose estimated execution cost exceeds a configured limit.
  • Persisted Queries: Restrict production clients to approved or registered operations when the architecture supports this model.
  • Rate Limiting: Limit requests based on factors such as identity, IP address, operation, or estimated query cost.
  • Resource Limits: Apply appropriate timeouts, pagination limits, concurrency limits, and database protections.
  • Introspection Controls: Consider restricting introspection in public production environments based on the organization's security and developer-access requirements.

title: Why and when should you disable GraphQL Introspection?
answer:
GraphQL Introspection allows clients and developer tools to discover the API's schema, including available types, fields, arguments, and directives.

For a public production API, an organization may choose to restrict or disable introspection to reduce the amount of information exposed to unauthenticated users. This can make automated schema discovery more difficult.

However, disabling introspection is not a replacement for authentication, authorization, rate limiting, query complexity controls, or other API security measures. Many internal or authenticated production environments intentionally keep introspection enabled for development and operational tooling.

title: Explain GraphQL Subscriptions and how they operate over WebSockets.
answer:
GraphQL Subscriptions provide a mechanism for receiving real-time, push-based updates from a GraphQL server.

The client establishes a persistent connection, commonly using WebSockets and a protocol such as graphql-ws. The client registers a subscription operation, and the server associates it with an appropriate event or Pub/Sub source.

When a relevant event occurs, the server resolves the subscription fields and sends the resulting GraphQL payload to the connected client.

This is useful for scenarios such as chat messages, live notifications, real-time dashboards, and collaborative applications.

title: Compare Subscriptions vs @defer and @stream directives.
answer:
• Subscriptions: Provide long-lived event streams where new data can be pushed to the client whenever relevant events occur.
  • @defer: Allows selected non-critical parts of a query response to be delivered later instead of blocking the initial response. This can improve perceived performance for queries containing slow or optional fields.
  • @stream: Allows items from a list field to be delivered incrementally as they become available rather than waiting for the complete list.

Subscriptions are designed for ongoing real-time updates, while @defer and @stream are designed for incremental delivery of a single query response.

title: How do you structure Error Handling in GraphQL?
answer:
GraphQL responses can contain both a data field and an errors array. This allows a query to return partial data when some fields fail while providing details about the errors.

Applications can use the extensions object to provide machine-readable metadata such as application-specific error codes.

{
  "data": {
    "user": null
  },
  "errors": [
    {
      "message": "Not Authorized",
      "path": ["user"],
      "extensions": {
        "code": "UNAUTHENTICATED"
      }
    }
  ]
}

Clients can use the error code and path to determine how the UI should respond without relying only on human-readable error messages.

title: How do you handle optimistic UI updates in Apollo Client?
answer:
Optimistic UI updates allow the application to update the interface immediately instead of waiting for a mutation's network response.

With Apollo Client, a mutation can provide an optimisticResponse that represents the expected successful result. Apollo temporarily writes this data into its normalized cache, allowing the UI to update immediately.

When the actual server response arrives, Apollo reconciles the optimistic data with the real response. If the mutation fails, the optimistic update is removed and the cache returns to the appropriate server-backed state.

title: What is the AST (Abstract Syntax Tree) in GraphQL, and how can server plugins inspect it?
answer:
The GraphQL AST (Abstract Syntax Tree) is a tree representation of a parsed GraphQL document. It contains nodes representing operations, fields, arguments, fragments, directives, and other parts of the query.

Server plugins, validation rules, middleware, and analysis tools can traverse the AST using visitor-style traversal to inspect the requested fields, arguments, directives, and nesting structure before or during execution.

This enables features such as query complexity analysis, depth limiting, logging, authorization checks, and query instrumentation.

title: How do you handle schema breaking changes safely in GraphQL enterprise deployment?
answer:
GraphQL APIs should generally evolve without immediately removing fields that existing clients may still depend on.

  • Avoid direct deletion or renaming: Introduce a replacement field first.
  • Use @deprecated: Mark the old field with a reason explaining what clients should use instead.
  • Monitor field usage: Track which clients and applications are still requesting the deprecated field.
  • Communicate migration timelines: Give consumers enough time to migrate.
  • Remove only after validation: Once production metrics confirm that active consumers have migrated, the deprecated field can be safely removed.

title: What is the role of Apollo Client's TypePolicies and read/merge functions?
answer:
TypePolicies allow Apollo Client to customize how types are identified, read, and merged in the normalized cache.

A read function can compute or expose a field from existing cached data without necessarily fetching it from the server.

A merge function controls how incoming field data is combined with existing cached data. This is particularly useful for pagination, where newly fetched pages need to be appended to previously cached items rather than replacing the entire list.

title: How do you test GraphQL Resolvers in isolation?
answer:
GraphQL resolvers are typically plain functions that receive parameters such as parent, args, context, and info. Because of this, they can be unit tested without starting an HTTP server.

Mock the resolver's dependencies through the context, such as database clients, authentication information, external services, and authorization services. Then provide representative arguments and assert that the resolver returns the expected result or error.

This produces fast unit tests that focus specifically on resolver behavior.

title: Explain how to manage local application state using GraphQL client state.
answer:
GraphQL clients such as Apollo Client can manage certain local application state alongside remote GraphQL data using their local cache capabilities.

Local fields can be read from the client cache and updated through cache operations or client-side state mechanisms. This allows application code to work with a unified data-access model while keeping purely client-side values separate from server-owned data.

For example, an application can maintain local values such as authentication UI state or theme information in its client-side state and query them alongside other application data.

query GetAppState {
  isLoggedIn
  theme
}

title: What is the Virtual DOM, and how does React’s reconciliation algorithm (Fiber) work?
answer:
The Virtual DOM is a lightweight JavaScript representation of the UI that React uses to describe what the rendered interface should look like. When state or props change, React creates a new element tree and compares it with the previous one during reconciliation.

Modern React uses the Fiber architecture as its reconciliation engine. Fiber represents components and their work as units that React can schedule. During the Render Phase, React determines what changed and builds a work-in-progress Fiber tree. This work can be prioritized, paused, restarted, or abandoned when appropriate.

During the Commit Phase, React applies the necessary DOM mutations synchronously. This architecture enables features such as concurrent rendering, transitions, and prioritization of urgent updates.

title: What is JSX, and what does it compile down to under the hood?
answer:
JSX is a JavaScript syntax extension that allows developers to describe UI using an HTML-like syntax directly inside JavaScript or TypeScript.

JSX is not understood directly by JavaScript engines. A compiler such as Babel or the TypeScript compiler transforms JSX into JavaScript calls that create React elements.

With the modern JSX transform, JSX is typically compiled using functions from react/jsx-runtime, such as jsx() and jsxs().

const element = <h1>Hello</h1>;

Conceptually, this becomes something similar to:

const element = jsx("h1", { children: "Hello" });

The resulting React element describes the UI that React should render.

title: Compare class components and functional components. Why did the industry shift toward functional components?
answer:
Class components use ES6 classes and React lifecycle methods such as componentDidMount, componentDidUpdate, and componentWillUnmount. State is managed using this.state and this.setState().

Functional components are JavaScript functions that return React elements. With Hooks such as useState, useEffect, useContext, and custom Hooks, functional components can manage state and side effects without classes.

The industry shifted toward functional components because they provide simpler syntax, avoid class-specific concepts such as this, make stateful logic easier to reuse through custom Hooks, and work naturally with modern React features.

title: What is the difference between props and state? Are props mutable?
answer:
Props are inputs passed from a parent component to a child component. They allow components to receive configuration or data from their parent.

State is data managed by a component or another state-management mechanism. When React state changes through its update mechanism, React can schedule a re-render.

Props should be treated as read-only by the receiving component. A child should not directly mutate its props. If the value needs to change, the parent should update the corresponding state and pass the new value down as props.

title: What are React Synthetic Events, and how do they differ from native browser DOM events?
answer:
SyntheticEvent is React's event abstraction that provides a consistent event interface across supported browsers.

React event handlers such as onClick and onChange receive React event objects rather than exposing browser-specific event behavior directly.

React also manages event delegation internally. In React 17 and later, event delegation is attached to the React root container rather than the document as in older React versions.

When access to the underlying browser event is required, the native event can be accessed through the SyntheticEvent's nativeEvent property.

title: What is lifting state up in React, and when should you use it?
answer:
Lifting state up means moving shared state from child components into their closest common parent component.

The parent becomes the single source of truth and passes the current state and event handlers to its children through props.

For example, if two sibling components need to stay synchronized, their shared state can be moved into their parent. This allows both children to receive consistent data and communicate changes through callbacks.

Use this pattern when multiple components need to coordinate or share the same piece of state. For state shared across many distant components, Context or an external state-management solution may be more appropriate.

title: Explain the difference between controlled and uncontrolled components.
answer:
A controlled component has its important form value managed by React state. The input receives its value through a prop and reports changes through an event handler.

const [value, setValue] = useState('');

<input
  value={value}
  onChange={e => setValue(e.target.value)}
/>

An uncontrolled component allows the DOM to maintain the current value. React can access the value using a ref when needed.

const inputRef = useRef(null);

<input ref={inputRef} defaultValue="Hello" />

Controlled components are useful when the application needs to validate, format, or react to every input change. Uncontrolled components can be useful for simpler forms, file inputs, or integrations with non-React DOM code.

title: Why should you avoid using array indices as key props when rendering lists?
answer:
React uses the key prop to identify elements between renders. Array indices are unstable when a list can be inserted into, deleted from, or reordered.

For example, if the first item is removed, the item that was previously at index 1 now has key 0. React may interpret it as the same element that previously had key 0 and reuse its component state and DOM.

This can cause bugs such as incorrect input values, lost focus, or state being associated with the wrong item. Stable, unique identifiers from the data should generally be used instead.

title: What are React Fragments, and why are they preferable to wrapping elements in <div> tags?
answer:
React Fragments allow a component to return multiple elements without introducing an additional DOM element.

<>
  <Header />
  <Content />
  <Footer />
</>

This is preferable to adding unnecessary <div> elements because Fragments do not create extra DOM nodes. This keeps the DOM structure cleaner and can prevent problems with CSS layouts, selectors, semantic HTML, and accessibility.

When a key is required, the explicit React.Fragment syntax can be used:

<React.Fragment key={item.id}>
  ...
</React.Fragment>

title: What is Strict Mode in React, and what side effects does it intentionally introduce in development?
answer:
Strict Mode is a development-only feature that helps identify potential problems in React applications. It does not render a visible UI element and does not affect the production build in the same way.

In modern React development, Strict Mode may intentionally invoke certain rendering logic more than once and perform an additional setup-and-cleanup cycle for effects. This helps detect impure rendering logic and missing cleanup for resources such as timers, subscriptions, event listeners, and WebSocket connections.

For example, an effect may follow a development sequence similar to setup → cleanup → setup. Developers should write effects so that cleanup correctly reverses the setup.

title: Explain the rules of React Hooks and why they cannot be called inside loops or conditional statements.
answer:
React Hooks must follow two main rules:

  • Hooks must be called only at the top level of React function components or custom Hooks.
  • Hooks must not be called inside loops, conditions, nested functions, or event handlers.

React relies on the consistent order of Hook calls to associate each Hook with its internal state and effect information. If the order changes between renders, React can associate state with the wrong Hook, resulting in errors or incorrect behavior.

// Correct
function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

  if (count > 10) {
    // Conditional logic can use the state,
    // but the Hook itself remains at the top level.
  }

  return <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>{count}</button>;
}

title: How does useEffect work, and how do you emulate componentDidMount, componentDidUpdate, and componentWillUnmount using it?
answer:
useEffect lets a function component synchronize with external systems such as APIs, subscriptions, timers, browser APIs, or other side effects. React runs the effect after the component has committed its rendered output.

The dependency array controls when the effect is re-executed:

  • componentDidMount-like behavior: Use an empty dependency array. useEffect(() => { ... }, []) runs after the initial mount, with the usual caveat that development Strict Mode can run setup and cleanup more than once.
  • componentDidUpdate-like behavior: Provide dependencies. The effect runs after the initial render and again when one of those dependencies changes.
  • componentWillUnmount-like cleanup: Return a cleanup function from the effect. React calls it when the component unmounts and before the effect is re-run because its dependencies changed.
useEffect(() => {
  const subscription = subscribe(id);

  return () => {
    subscription.unsubscribe();
  };
}, [id]);

title: What is the difference between useMemo and useCallback? Give practical examples for each.
answer:
useMemo memoizes the result of a calculation, while useCallback memoizes a function reference.

useMemo practical example: Use it when an expensive calculation should not be repeated unless its dependencies change.

const filteredProducts = useMemo(() => {
  return products.filter(product => product.name.includes(search));
}, [products, search]);

useCallback practical example: Use it when a stable callback reference is useful, such as when passing a callback to a memoized child component.

const handleSelect = useCallback((id) => {
  setSelectedId(id);
}, []);

Both should be used based on actual performance needs rather than automatically memoizing every value or function.

title: How does useRef differ from useState, and why doesn't mutating useRef.current trigger a re-render?
answer:
useState stores data that participates in React's rendering process. Updating state through its setter schedules React to process an update and potentially re-render the component.

useRef returns a stable object whose current property can be changed without scheduling a React render.

const countRef = useRef(0);

countRef.current += 1;

Changing ref.current does not trigger a re-render because React does not use ref mutations as a signal that the UI needs to be recalculated. Refs are useful for DOM references, timer IDs, previous values, and other mutable values that do not directly determine the rendered UI.

title: Compare useLayoutEffect and useEffect. When would you choose useLayoutEffect?
answer:
useEffect runs after React commits the DOM and generally after the browser has painted. It is appropriate for most side effects, such as data fetching, subscriptions, logging, and synchronization with external systems.

useLayoutEffect runs synchronously after React has applied DOM mutations but before the browser paints. Because it can block painting, it should be used only when necessary.

Use useLayoutEffect when you need to measure the DOM or make a visual adjustment before the user sees the result. Common examples include measuring an element's dimensions, positioning a tooltip or popover, or preventing a visible layout flicker.

title: How does useReducer work, and when should you use it instead of useState?
answer:
useReducer manages state using a reducer function that receives the current state and an action and returns the next state.

const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, initialState);

dispatch({ type: 'increment' });

The reducer follows the general pattern:

function reducer(state, action) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case 'increment':
      return { ...state, count: state.count + 1 };
    default:
      return state;
  }
}

useReducer is useful when state contains multiple related values, when many state transitions exist, or when the update logic is complex and benefits from being centralized and explicit. For simple independent values, useState is usually easier.

title: What is Prop Drilling, and how do Context API or state libraries such as Redux Toolkit and Zustand solve it?
answer:
Prop Drilling occurs when data must be passed through multiple intermediate components even though those components do not need the data themselves.

Context API allows a value to be provided by an ancestor and consumed by descendant components without explicitly passing it through every intermediate component.

const UserContext = createContext(null);

<UserContext.Provider value={user}>
  <App />
</UserContext.Provider>

State libraries such as Redux Toolkit and Zustand provide external stores that components can subscribe to. They are useful when state is shared widely, has complex update logic, or requires features such as selectors, middleware, persistence, or developer tooling.

title: How do you prevent unnecessary re-renders in Context API providers?
answer:
Context consumers can re-render when the provider's value changes identity. Several techniques can reduce unnecessary updates:

  • Memoize the provider value: Use useMemo when the value is an object or contains derived data.
  • Memoize callbacks: Use useCallback when functions are part of the Context value and their identity does not need to change.
  • Split large contexts: Separate unrelated values into focused contexts, such as UserContext and ThemeContext.
  • Keep state local when possible: Avoid putting state into Context when only one small part of the component tree needs it.
  • Use an external store for high-frequency shared state: Libraries with selectors can allow components to subscribe to specific state slices.
const value = useMemo(() => ({
  user,
  logout
}), [user, logout]);

return (
  <UserContext.Provider value={value}>
    {children}
  </UserContext.Provider>
);

title: How do you create and structure a custom React Hook for reusable data fetching?
answer:
A reusable data-fetching Hook should encapsulate request state and expose a simple interface such as data, loading, and error. It should also handle cleanup so that obsolete requests do not update state after the component unmounts or the URL changes.

function useFetch(url) {
  const [data, setData] = useState(null);
  const [loading, setLoading] = useState(false);
  const [error, setError] = useState(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    const controller = new AbortController();

    async function fetchData() {
      try {
        setLoading(true);
        setError(null);

        const response = await fetch(url, {
          signal: controller.signal
        });

        if (!response.ok) {
          throw new Error('Request failed');
        }

        const result = await response.json();
        setData(result);
      } catch (err) {
        if (err.name !== 'AbortError') {
          setError(err);
        }
      } finally {
        setLoading(false);
      }
    }

    fetchData();

    return () => controller.abort();
  }, [url]);

  return { data, loading, error };
}

For production applications with caching, retries, deduplication, pagination, and background revalidation, a dedicated data-fetching library such as TanStack Query can often be preferable to building all of these behaviors manually.

title: What is useImperativeHandle, and how is it used alongside forwardRef?
answer:
useImperativeHandle allows a component to customize the value exposed through a ref. Instead of exposing the complete underlying DOM node, the child can expose a small, explicit API such as focus() or reset().

It is commonly used with ref forwarding so that the parent can obtain the child component's imperative API.

const Input = forwardRef(function Input(props, ref) {
  const inputRef = useRef(null);

  useImperativeHandle(ref, () => ({
    focus() {
      inputRef.current?.focus();
    },
    reset() {
      if (inputRef.current) {
        inputRef.current.value = '';
      }
    }
  }), []);

  return <input ref={inputRef} {...props} />;
});

The parent can then call the exposed methods through its ref. This pattern should be used sparingly because React generally favors declarative data flow through props and state.

title: What are Higher-Order Components (HOCs), and how do they compare to Custom Hooks?
answer:
A Higher-Order Component (HOC) is a function that accepts a React component and returns a new enhanced component.

const EnhancedComponent = withAuth(MyComponent);

HOCs were commonly used to reuse cross-cutting logic such as authentication, permissions, subscriptions, and data loading.

Custom Hooks provide a more modern way to reuse stateful logic without adding wrapper components to the component tree.

Custom Hooks are generally easier to compose and avoid problems associated with HOCs such as wrapper nesting, prop collisions, hidden dependencies, and complicated component trees. HOCs are still useful in some legacy codebases and specific component-enhancement scenarios.

title: Explain Component Composition vs. Inheritance in React.
answer:
Composition means building complex components by combining smaller components and passing behavior or UI through props, children, or specialized components.

function Dialog({ children }) {
  return <div className="dialog">{children}</div>;
}

<Dialog>
  <LoginForm />
</Dialog>

Inheritance would involve creating a child class that extends another component or class. React generally favors composition over inheritance for sharing UI behavior and structure.

Composition provides greater flexibility and keeps components loosely coupled. React's model is designed around composing components rather than building deep inheritance hierarchies.

title: What is Error Boundary in React, and why can’t functional components act as error boundaries directly yet?
answer:
An Error Boundary is a React component that catches JavaScript errors thrown during rendering and certain lifecycle operations in its descendant component tree. It can log the error and display a fallback UI instead of allowing the affected part of the application to crash.

Error Boundaries are implemented using the supported class-component lifecycle APIs static getDerivedStateFromError() and/or componentDidCatch().

React does not currently provide a Hook equivalent that allows a normal functional component to implement the Error Boundary mechanism directly. Functional components can still exist inside an Error Boundary.

class ErrorBoundary extends React.Component {
  state = { hasError: false };

  static getDerivedStateFromError() {
    return { hasError: true };
  }

  componentDidCatch(error, info) {
    console.error(error, info);
  }

  render() {
    if (this.state.hasError) {
      return <h1>Something went wrong.</h1>;
    }

    return this.props.children;
  }
}

title: How does code splitting work in React using React.lazy and Suspense?
answer:
Code splitting divides an application's JavaScript bundle into smaller chunks that can be loaded when they are needed instead of downloading the entire application upfront.

React.lazy() allows a component to be loaded dynamically using a JavaScript import(). The lazy component must be rendered inside a Suspense boundary that displays fallback UI while the chunk is loading.

const Dashboard = React.lazy(() => import('./Dashboard'));

function App() {
  return (
    <Suspense fallback={<div>Loading...</div>}>
      <Dashboard />
    </Suspense>
  );
}

Code splitting is commonly applied at route boundaries and for large features such as editors, charts, dashboards, and rarely used dialogs.

title: Explain the concept of Concurrent React features like useTransition and useDeferredValue.
answer:
Concurrent React allows React to work on rendering without requiring every update to block the browser until the entire render is complete. This enables React to prioritize urgent work and defer less important rendering work.

useTransition lets you mark a state update as non-urgent and provides an isPending indicator.

const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition();

startTransition(() => {
  setSearchResults(results);
});

useDeferredValue accepts a value and returns a deferred version that can temporarily lag behind the current value while React handles more urgent updates.

const deferredQuery = useDeferredValue(query);

The main distinction is that useTransition marks an update as non-urgent, while useDeferredValue lets a value have a lower-priority representation.

title: What is the difference between client-side state and server/cache state such as TanStack Query or React Query?
answer:
Client-side state represents information primarily owned and controlled by the browser application, such as modal visibility, selected tabs, form state, UI preferences, and temporary interaction state. It can be managed with useState, useReducer, Context, Zustand, Redux Toolkit, or similar solutions.

Server/cache state represents data owned by a remote server that the client temporarily stores and synchronizes locally. Examples include users, products, orders, and API responses.

Libraries such as TanStack Query provide functionality specifically for server state, including caching, request deduplication, background refetching, retries, stale-data management, pagination, and mutation handling.

Separating these concerns prevents a general-purpose client-state store from becoming responsible for complex server-data synchronization logic.

title: How does React handle batching updates (auto-batching in React 18+)?
answer:
Batching means React groups multiple state updates together and processes them as a single rendering update when possible.

Before React 18, automatic batching primarily applied to updates triggered inside React event handlers. Updates in asynchronous callbacks such as promises and timers could result in separate renders.

With React 18 and the modern root API, automatic batching also applies to updates from promises, timers, native event handlers, and other asynchronous contexts.

setCount(c => c + 1);
setFlag(true);

// React can process these updates together.

When an application specifically needs a synchronous DOM update, React provides flushSync to force an update to be flushed immediately.

title: What are Portals in React (createPortal), and what are their typical use cases?
answer:
React Portals allow React children to be rendered into a DOM node outside their normal DOM hierarchy while remaining part of the same React component tree.

createPortal(child, container);

Portals are commonly used for:

  • Modal dialogs
  • Dropdown menus
  • Tooltips and popovers
  • Toast notifications
  • Context menus
  • UI that needs to escape an ancestor's overflow or stacking context

Although the DOM location changes, React event propagation follows the React tree, so events from a portal can bubble to React ancestors.

title: How do you profile and debug performance bottlenecks in a large React application?
answer:
Performance debugging should begin by measuring the application rather than adding memoization blindly.

  • React DevTools Profiler: Identify components that render frequently or take significant time to render.
  • Chrome DevTools Performance panel: Inspect long tasks, scripting, layout, painting, and browser rendering activity.
  • React DevTools Components panel: Inspect props, state, component hierarchy, and render behavior.
  • Network tools: Identify slow API requests, large payloads, duplicate requests, and inefficient caching.
  • Bundle analysis: Identify large JavaScript dependencies and opportunities for code splitting or tree-shaking.
  • Web Vitals: Monitor metrics such as LCP, INP, and CLS to understand real user performance.

After identifying the bottleneck, optimize the actual cause using techniques such as memoization, virtualization, code splitting, state restructuring, request caching, image optimization, or moving expensive work off the main thread.

title: What are React Server Components (RSC), and how do they differ from traditional Client Components?
answer:
React Server Components (RSC) are components that execute on the server and whose component implementation does not need to be sent to the browser as client-side JavaScript.

Server Components can access server-side resources such as databases or files within the server environment and can reduce the amount of JavaScript required by the client. They cannot use client-only features such as interactive event handlers, browser APIs, or client-side state Hooks such as useState.

Client Components are components whose code is sent to the browser and can use state, effects, event handlers, and browser APIs. Frameworks such as Next.js allow Server and Client Components to be composed together.
