The key distinction is that RSCs execute on the server as part of the server component model, while Client Components execute in the browser and provide interactivity.

title: What are the key differences between Next.js Pages Router (/pages) and App Router (/app)?
answer:
The Pages Router is the older Next.js routing system based on files inside the /pages directory. It uses APIs such as getServerSideProps, getStaticProps, and getStaticPaths for server-side and static data fetching.

The App Router, introduced in Next.js 13, is based on the /app directory and uses React Server Components by default. It provides nested layouts, loading and error UI, route groups, parallel routes, intercepting routes, Server Actions, and newer data-fetching and caching APIs.

In the App Router, components are Server Components by default. A component must use the 'use client' directive when it needs client-side state, effects, event handlers, or browser APIs.

title: Explain dynamic route segments and catch-all routes ([...slug] vs [[...slug]]) in Next.js.
answer:
A dynamic route segment uses square brackets to capture part of the URL.

For example, app/products/[id]/page.tsx matches URLs such as /products/123, where id is available as a route parameter.

A catch-all segment such as [...slug] captures multiple path segments and requires at least one segment. For example, app/docs/[...slug]/page.tsx can match /docs/react/hooks.

An optional catch-all segment such as [[...slug]] can match both the base route and routes containing additional segments. For example, it can match both /docs and /docs/react/hooks.

title: How do Parallel Routes (@folder) and Intercepting Routes ((.)folder) work in the App Router?
answer:
Parallel Routes use named slots represented by folders such as @dashboard or @modal. They allow multiple route segments to be rendered simultaneously within the same layout. This is useful for dashboards, split views, and independently loading UI sections.

Intercepting Routes use conventions such as (.), (..), or related segment notation to render another route within the current layout context. A common use case is opening a detail page as a modal when navigating from a list while still allowing the detail route to work as a normal full page when accessed directly.

Together, these features enable sophisticated UI patterns such as modal routing, dashboards, side-by-side views, and independently navigable sections.

title: What is the purpose of layout.js, page.js, loading.js, error.js, and not-found.js in the App Router?
answer:
• layout.js: Defines shared UI for a route segment and its child routes. Layouts can persist across navigation and can be nested.
  • page.js: Defines the UI for a specific route and makes that route accessible.
  • loading.js: Defines a loading UI that Next.js can display while the route segment is loading.
  • error.js: Defines an error boundary UI for handling errors in a route segment. It is a Client Component.
  • not-found.js: Defines the UI displayed when a route or requested resource cannot be found, typically when notFound() is invoked.

These file conventions allow routing, layouts, loading states, errors, and not-found states to be colocated with the route they belong to.

title: How does Middleware work in Next.js, and where is it executed?
answer:
Next.js Middleware allows code to run before a request is completed. It can inspect the incoming request and perform actions such as redirects, rewrites, authentication checks, localization, or request-based routing decisions.

Middleware is defined in a project-level middleware.ts or middleware.js file and can be restricted to specific paths using a matcher configuration.

It runs in the Next.js server/request processing environment, historically associated with the Edge Runtime. The exact runtime capabilities depend on the Next.js version and configuration, so middleware should avoid APIs that are unavailable in its configured runtime.

title: Compare Server-Side Rendering (SSR), Static Site Generation (SSG), Incremental Static Regeneration (ISR), and Client-Side Rendering (CSR).
answer:
• SSR: HTML is generated on the server for a request and returned to the client. It is useful for dynamic data that must be rendered per request.
  • SSG: HTML is generated ahead of time and can be served from a cache or CDN. It is suitable for content that does not need to change for every request.
  • ISR: Pages can be statically generated and then regenerated after a configured revalidation period or when explicitly invalidated. This combines many benefits of static generation with fresher data.
  • CSR: The browser downloads JavaScript and renders or updates the UI on the client, commonly after an initial HTML shell is delivered.

The appropriate strategy depends on data freshness, SEO requirements, request-specific information, infrastructure, and performance goals.

title: How does data fetching differ in the Pages Router (getServerSideProps, getStaticProps) vs. the App Router (async Server Components with fetch)?
answer:
In the Pages Router, getServerSideProps fetches data on the server for each request, while getStaticProps fetches data during the build process for statically generated pages. getStaticPaths is used to specify dynamic paths that should be generated statically.

In the App Router, Server Components can be asynchronous and can fetch data directly during server rendering.

export default async function Page() {
  const response = await fetch('https://api.example.com/products');
  const products = await response.json();

  return <ProductList products={products} />;
}

The App Router integrates data fetching with React Server Components and Next.js caching and revalidation mechanisms rather than requiring a dedicated getServerSideProps or getStaticProps function.

title: What is Incremental Static Regeneration (ISR), and how do time-based revalidation and path-based revalidation (revalidatePath / revalidateTag) work?
answer:
Incremental Static Regeneration (ISR) allows statically generated content to be updated after deployment without rebuilding the entire application.

Time-based revalidation specifies how long cached data or a route can remain valid before Next.js revalidates it.

fetch('https://api.example.com/products', {
  next: { revalidate: 60 }
});

revalidatePath() invalidates cached data associated with a specific route path so that it can be regenerated or refreshed.

revalidatePath('/products');

revalidateTag() invalidates cached data associated with a cache tag. This is useful when multiple pages depend on the same underlying data.

revalidateTag('products');

These mechanisms allow applications to balance freshness and performance without rebuilding every page for every data change.

title: What are Server Actions in Next.js, and how do they simplify form processing and state updates?
answer:
Server Actions are asynchronous server-side functions that can be invoked from supported Server or Client Component workflows. They are commonly used for mutations such as creating records, updating data, deleting resources, and processing forms.

A Server Action can be connected directly to a form's action attribute, allowing form data to be processed on the server without manually creating a separate API route for every mutation.

'use server';

export async function createUser(formData) {
  const name = formData.get('name');
  await db.user.create({ data: { name } });
}

When combined with React APIs such as useActionState and useFormStatus, Server Actions can simplify pending states, validation results, and server-side form mutations.

title: What is hydration in Next.js, and how do you resolve Hydration Mismatch errors?
answer:
Hydration is the process where React attaches client-side behavior and event handlers to HTML that was already rendered on the server.

A hydration mismatch occurs when the server-rendered HTML does not match the markup produced by the client's initial React render.

Common causes include rendering window or document values during the initial render, using Date.now() or random values, relying on different data between server and client, browser-only state such as localStorage, and invalid HTML nesting.

To resolve the issue, make the initial server and client output deterministic, move browser-only logic into useEffect when appropriate, use client-only rendering when necessary, and ensure the server and client use the same initial data.

title: How does the next/image component optimize images?
answer:
The next/image component provides image optimization features such as responsive sizing, automatic image resizing, lazy loading for appropriate images, and delivery of modern image formats supported by the configured image optimization pipeline.

Next.js can generate appropriately sized images based on the requested dimensions and device characteristics, reducing unnecessary network transfer.

Developers should provide appropriate dimensions or use the supported responsive layout features so the browser can reserve space for the image and reduce layout shifts.

import Image from 'next/image';

<Image
  src="/hero.jpg"
  alt="Hero image"
  width={1200}
  height={600}
/>

title: How does next/font eliminate layout shifts (CLS) when loading custom web fonts?
answer:
next/font integrates font loading into the Next.js build and rendering pipeline. It can optimize font delivery and automatically apply font-related CSS so the browser has predictable font metrics before the page is displayed.

By reducing late font swaps and avoiding unnecessary external font requests, next/font helps prevent visible text reflow and improve Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS).

import { Inter } from 'next/font/google';

const inter = Inter({ subsets: ['latin'] });

export default function Layout({ children }) {
  return <body className={inter.className}>{children}</body>;
}

Next.js also supports local fonts through next/font/local.

title: What strategies does Next.js use for Script Optimization using next/script?
answer:
The next/script component provides controlled loading strategies for third-party scripts so they do not unnecessarily block the initial page rendering.

Common strategies include:

  • beforeInteractive: Loads a script before the page becomes interactive. It should be reserved for scripts that are essential before interaction.
  • afterInteractive: Loads the script after the page becomes interactive. This is a common choice for analytics and other non-critical scripts.
  • lazyOnload: Loads the script during browser idle time after the page has loaded, making it suitable for low-priority scripts.
  • worker: In supported configurations, can move certain third-party scripts to a Web Worker to reduce main-thread work.

Choosing the appropriate strategy helps reduce blocking JavaScript and improve page performance.

title: How do you configure SEO and dynamic Open Graph meta tags using the Metadata API in the App Router?
answer:
The App Router provides a Metadata API for defining page metadata such as titles, descriptions, canonical information, robots directives, and Open Graph data.

Static metadata can be exported from a layout or page:

export const metadata = {
  title: 'Products',
  description: 'Browse our products',
  openGraph: {
    title: 'Products',
    description: 'Browse our products'
  }
};

For dynamic routes, generateMetadata() can generate metadata using route parameters or fetched data.

export async function generateMetadata({ params }) {
  const product = await getProduct(params.id);

  return {
    title: product.name,
    description: product.description,
    openGraph: {
      title: product.name,
      description: product.description,
      images: [product.image]
    }
  };
}

title: How does Next.js handle extended fetch caching and Request Deduplication?
answer:
In the App Router, Next.js integrates data fetching with its server-side caching and revalidation mechanisms. Depending on the Next.js version, request configuration, and rendering context, a fetch can participate in the Next.js Data Cache or be treated as dynamic.

Options such as next.revalidate can provide time-based revalidation, while cache: 'no-store' can request fresh data for a fetch.

const response = await fetch(url, {
  next: { revalidate: 60 }
});

Next.js and React can also avoid redundant work when identical data requests occur during the same rendering process. The exact caching and request-memoization behavior depends on the API and Next.js version, so application code should not assume that every fetch is globally cached indefinitely.

title: What are Route Handlers (route.ts), and how do they replace traditional API routes?
answer:
Route Handlers are the App Router's mechanism for creating custom HTTP endpoints using files such as app/api/users/route.ts.

They use standard Web Request and Response APIs and can export functions corresponding to HTTP methods such as GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE.

export async function GET() {
  const users = await getUsers();
  return Response.json(users);
}

export async function POST(request) {
  const body = await request.json();
  const user = await createUser(body);
  return Response.json(user, { status: 201 });
}

They provide an App Router alternative to the API Route files traditionally used under pages/api.

title: How do environment variables work in Next.js (NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix vs server-only)?
answer:
Next.js distinguishes between server-only environment variables and variables that are intentionally exposed to browser-side code.

Variables without the NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix are intended for server-side use and should be treated as secrets when they contain sensitive values such as database credentials or private API keys.

Variables prefixed with NEXT_PUBLIC_ can be included in the client-side JavaScript bundle and should therefore be considered public.

DATABASE_URL=postgres://...
NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL=https://api.example.com

Never put passwords, private tokens, or other secrets in NEXT_PUBLIC_ variables because exposing them makes them accessible to users of the application.

title: What is static export (output: 'export'), and what features are disabled when using it?
answer:
Setting output: 'export' configures Next.js to generate a fully static version of the application that can be deployed to static hosting without a Next.js server.

// next.config.js
const nextConfig = {
  output: 'export'
};

module.exports = nextConfig;

Because there is no Next.js server at runtime, features that require server execution are unavailable or require alternative implementations. These include request-time server rendering, Server Actions, Route Handlers, Middleware, and other server-dependent behavior. Dynamic routes must also be statically renderable at build time.

Static export is well suited to sites that can be completely generated ahead of time and hosted on a CDN or static web server.

title: How do you handle authentication such as NextAuth.js / Auth.js with JWTs and session management across client and server?
answer:
Authentication libraries such as Auth.js provide mechanisms for handling login flows, providers, sessions, cookies, and authorization in Next.js applications.

With a JWT-based session strategy, session information can be encoded in a signed token that is typically stored in a secure, HTTP-only cookie. Server-side code can read and validate the session without exposing sensitive authentication tokens to browser JavaScript.

Client Components can use the authentication library's client-side session APIs when they need to display authenticated UI, while Server Components, Route Handlers, or Server Actions can perform server-side authorization checks before accessing protected resources.

Authentication establishes who the user is; authorization must still be enforced for each protected operation or resource.

title: How do you optimize bundle size in a Next.js application using dynamic imports (next/dynamic)?
answer:
next/dynamic allows components to be loaded dynamically so their JavaScript can be split into separate chunks instead of being included in the initial bundle.

import dynamic from 'next/dynamic';

const HeavyChart = dynamic(() => import('./HeavyChart'), {
  loading: () => <p>Loading chart...</p>
});

This is useful for large or infrequently used components such as charts, rich text editors, maps, analytics dashboards, and modal workflows.

When a component depends on browser-only APIs, dynamic imports can also be configured with ssr: false where appropriate:

const ClientOnlyWidget = dynamic(
  () => import('./ClientOnlyWidget'),
  { ssr: false }
);

Bundle analyzers, route-level splitting, avoiding unnecessary dependencies, and importing only the required functions from libraries can further reduce JavaScript bundle size.

title: How do you handle internationalization (i18n) routing and localized content in Next.js?
answer:
Internationalization in Next.js can be implemented by representing the locale as part of the URL, such as /en/products and /fr/products, or by using middleware and an internationalization library to determine and route users to the appropriate locale.

In the App Router, a common structure is app/[locale]/..., where the locale becomes a dynamic route segment. Middleware can inspect the user's preferred language, cookie, or existing URL and redirect or rewrite requests to the appropriate locale.

Localized content can be loaded from translation files or a translation service. The application should also handle locale-aware formatting for dates, numbers, currencies, pluralization, and right-to-left languages when required.

title: How does streaming SSR with HTML Suspense boundaries work in Next.js?
answer:
Streaming SSR allows Next.js to send the server-rendered HTML to the browser incrementally instead of waiting for the entire page to finish rendering.

React Suspense boundaries divide the page into independently renderable sections. Next.js can send the initial shell and immediately available content first, while slower sections are streamed to the browser when their data or components become ready.

<Suspense fallback={<ProductSkeleton />}>
  <SlowProductList />
</Suspense>

This improves perceived performance because users can see useful content and loading placeholders without waiting for the slowest component to finish.

title: How do you configure Custom Headers, Redirects, and Rewrites in next.config.js?
answer:
Next.js provides configuration APIs in next.config.js for controlling HTTP headers and request routing behavior.

Headers can add response headers such as security policies:

async headers() {
  return [
    {
      source: '/(.*)',
      headers: [
        { key: 'X-Content-Type-Options', value: 'nosniff' }
      ]
    }
  ];
}

Redirects permanently or temporarily send users from one URL to another:

async redirects() {
  return [
    {
      source: '/old-page',
      destination: '/new-page',
      permanent: true
    }
  ];
}

Rewrites internally map one URL to another resource without changing the URL displayed in the browser. They are useful for proxying requests or mapping friendly URLs to internal routes.

title: How do you manage CORS and secure API routes in Next.js?
answer:
CORS should be configured on the server or Route Handler by allowing only trusted origins rather than using a broad wildcard when credentials or sensitive APIs are involved.

A secure Next.js API should also validate authentication and authorization on the server, validate request bodies and parameters, apply rate limiting where appropriate, avoid exposing secrets to Client Components, and use secure cookie settings when cookies are used for authentication.

For a Route Handler, response headers can be configured explicitly:

return new Response(JSON.stringify(data), {
  headers: {
    'Content-Type': 'application/json',
    'Access-Control-Allow-Origin': 'https://example.com'
  }
});

CORS is a browser access-control mechanism and should not be treated as an authentication or authorization mechanism.

title: What is Turbopack, and how does it compare to Webpack in modern Next.js development?
answer:
Turbopack is a high-performance JavaScript and TypeScript bundler developed by Vercel and written in Rust. It is designed for fast incremental compilation and development workflows in Next.js.

Webpack is a mature JavaScript bundler with a large ecosystem, extensive plugin support, and many years of production usage.

Turbopack focuses on fast startup, incremental rebuilds, and efficient development feedback, while Webpack provides a broader and more mature customization ecosystem. Modern Next.js versions increasingly use Turbopack for development, while the exact level of Turbopack support and production capabilities depends on the Next.js version and project configuration.

title: What is a RESTful API, and what are its key architectural constraints such as Statelessness and Uniform Interface?
answer:
A RESTful API is an API designed around the principles of Representational State Transfer (REST). It typically exposes resources through URLs and uses standard HTTP methods to operate on those resources.

Key REST constraints include:

  • Client-Server: The client and server have separate responsibilities.
  • Statelessness: Each request contains the information necessary for the server to process it. The server does not depend on stored client session state between requests.
  • Uniform Interface: Resources and operations follow consistent HTTP semantics.
  • Cacheability: Responses should indicate whether they can be cached.
  • Layered System: Clients do not necessarily know whether they are communicating directly with the origin server or an intermediary.
  • Code on Demand: An optional constraint allowing servers to transfer executable code to clients.

title: Explain the difference between HTTP methods: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE.
answer:
• GET: Retrieves a resource or collection of resources. It should not modify server state.
  • POST: Submits data to create a resource or trigger a server-side operation. Repeating the same request may produce multiple effects.
  • PUT: Replaces the representation of a resource at a known URI or creates it when the API defines that behavior.
  • PATCH: Applies a partial modification to an existing resource.
  • DELETE: Removes a resource or requests that it be removed.

The exact behavior depends on the API contract, but these methods have standardized HTTP semantics.

title: What is the difference between PUT and PATCH?
answer:
PUT is generally used to replace the representation of a resource with the supplied representation. The client typically sends the complete resource representation expected by the API.

PATCH is used for partial modifications, where the client sends only the fields that need to change.

PUT /users/123
{
  "name": "Mani",
  "email": "mani@example.com",
  "role": "developer"
}

PATCH /users/123
{
  "role": "admin"
}

PUT and PATCH have different semantics, and the exact update behavior should always be documented by the API.

title: What makes an HTTP method Idempotent vs Safe? Categorize GET, POST, PUT, and DELETE.
answer:
A safe HTTP method is intended not to change server state. An idempotent method produces the same intended server state when the same request is performed multiple times, although individual responses may differ.

  • GET: Safe and idempotent.
  • POST: Not safe and generally not idempotent.
  • PUT: Not safe, but idempotent.
  • DELETE: Not safe, but idempotent in HTTP semantics.

Idempotency is important for retry logic because an idempotent request can generally be retried without repeatedly applying the intended state change.

title: Explain HTTP Status Code ranges: 2xx, 3xx, 4xx, and 5xx. Give examples for 201, 204, 401, 403, 404, 409, 422, and 502.
answer:
• 2xx - Success: The request was successfully processed.
  • 3xx - Redirection: The client needs to follow a redirect or use cached information.
  • 4xx - Client Error: The request cannot be fulfilled because of a client-side issue.
  • 5xx - Server Error: The server or an upstream dependency failed while processing the request.

Important examples include:

  • 201 Created: A resource was successfully created.
  • 204 No Content: The request succeeded and there is no response body.
  • 401 Unauthorized: Authentication is required or the supplied authentication credentials are invalid.
  • 403 Forbidden: The server understood the request but refuses to authorize it.
  • 404 Not Found: The requested resource could not be found.
  • 409 Conflict: The request conflicts with the current state of the resource.
  • 422 Unprocessable Content: The request syntax is valid but the submitted content cannot be processed according to the API's rules.
  • 502 Bad Gateway: A gateway or proxy received an invalid response from an upstream server.

title: What is CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing), and how do preflight (OPTIONS) requests work?
answer:
CORS is a browser security mechanism that controls whether JavaScript running on one origin can access resources on another origin.

For simple cross-origin requests, the browser may send the request directly and then enforce the server's CORS response headers. For requests that are not considered simple, the browser first sends an OPTIONS preflight request to ask the server whether the actual request is permitted.

The preflight can include headers such as Origin, Access-Control-Request-Method, and Access-Control-Request-Headers. The server responds with headers such as Access-Control-Allow-Origin, Access-Control-Allow-Methods, and Access-Control-Allow-Headers.

If the browser determines that the request is allowed, it proceeds with the actual request.

title: How do you handle authentication in REST APIs using JWTs, Bearer Tokens, and HttpOnly cookies?
answer:
A common REST authentication flow uses a short-lived access token and, when required, a refresh mechanism.

With a Bearer Token, the client sends the access token in the Authorization header:

Authorization: Bearer <access-token>

A JWT is one possible token format. It is signed so the server can verify its integrity and may contain claims such as user ID, issuer, and expiration.

When using HttpOnly cookies, the browser automatically sends the cookie with matching requests, while JavaScript cannot read an HttpOnly cookie. Secure authentication cookies should generally use attributes such as Secure and an appropriate SameSite policy.

The appropriate approach depends on the application architecture. Authentication tokens should be short-lived where practical, and authorization must always be enforced server-side.

title: What is the difference between Axios and native fetch API for network requests?
answer:
fetch is a browser and JavaScript platform API that provides a standard interface for HTTP requests. It requires explicit handling for some conveniences, such as treating non-2xx responses as errors.

Axios is a third-party HTTP client that provides additional features such as request and response interceptors, automatic JSON transformation, configurable defaults, and convenient error handling.

Fetch has the advantage of being built into modern browsers and Node.js environments, while Axios can provide a richer abstraction for applications that need centralized HTTP behavior.

const response = await fetch('/api/users');

if (!response.ok) {
  throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`);
}

const data = await response.json();

title: How do you handle request cancellation in fetch using AbortController?
answer:
AbortController provides a standard mechanism for cancelling a fetch request.

const controller = new AbortController();

fetch('/api/search?q=react', {
  signal: controller.signal
});

controller.abort();

In React, the controller is commonly created inside an effect and aborted during cleanup. This is useful when a component unmounts or when a new search request makes the previous request obsolete.

useEffect(() => {
  const controller = new AbortController();

  fetch(url, { signal: controller.signal });

  return () => controller.abort();
}, [url]);

title: What strategies do you use for retrying failed requests, such as exponential backoff?
answer:
Retry logic should distinguish between transient failures and permanent failures. Network failures, timeouts, and some 5xx responses may be retryable, while many 4xx responses should not be retried automatically.

Exponential backoff increases the delay between retries, for example:

delay = baseDelay * 2 ** attempt

In production, add jitter to prevent many clients from retrying simultaneously. Respect the server's Retry-After header when provided, impose a maximum number of attempts, and use retries only for operations that are safe to repeat or are explicitly designed to be idempotent.

title: What is API rate limiting, and how should a front-end respond to HTTP 429 Too Many Requests?
answer:
API rate limiting restricts how many requests a client can make within a defined period. It protects services from abuse, accidental request storms, and resource exhaustion.

When the server returns 429 Too Many Requests, the front end should avoid immediately retrying in a tight loop. It should respect the Retry-After header when available, otherwise use an appropriate backoff strategy.

The UI can show a temporary message, disable repeated actions when appropriate, and avoid duplicate requests through debouncing, throttling, request deduplication, or client-side caching.

title: How do you implement global error handling and response interceptors in Axios/fetch?
answer:
With Axios, request and response interceptors can centralize behavior such as adding authentication headers, logging requests, transforming responses, and handling common HTTP errors.

axios.interceptors.response.use(
  response => response,
  error => {
    if (error.response?.status === 401) {
      // Handle expired authentication
    }
    return Promise.reject(error);
  }
);

With fetch, a reusable wrapper function can provide similar behavior:

async function apiFetch(url, options) {
  const response = await fetch(url, options);

  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new ApiError(response.status);
  }

  return response.json();
}

Global handling should centralize common behavior while still allowing individual features to handle domain-specific errors appropriately.

title: What are webhooks, and how do they differ from traditional REST polling?
answer:
Polling means the client repeatedly sends requests to an API asking whether something has changed. This can generate unnecessary traffic and introduce delays between an event occurring and the client discovering it.

A webhook reverses the communication flow. When an event occurs, the service sends an HTTP request to a preconfigured endpoint owned by the receiving application.

Webhooks are generally more efficient for event-driven integrations because the receiver does not need to repeatedly ask whether an event occurred. Webhook endpoints should validate authenticity, handle retries and duplicate deliveries, and process events idempotently.

title: How do you handle file uploads (multipart/form-data) from a front-end client?
answer:
For REST APIs that accept multipart uploads, the browser can use FormData to construct a multipart/form-data request.

const formData = new FormData();
formData.append('file', file);
formData.append('description', 'Profile image');

await fetch('/api/upload', {
  method: 'POST',
  body: formData
});

When using FormData with fetch, the application should normally not manually set the Content-Type header. The browser sets the multipart boundary automatically.

For large files, applications may use direct-to-object-storage uploads with pre-signed URLs, allowing the client to upload directly to storage rather than sending the entire file through the application server.

title: What is API versioning, such as URI path vs Header versioning, and why is it important?
answer:
API versioning allows an API to evolve while maintaining compatibility for existing consumers.

URI versioning places the version in the URL:

/api/v1/users
/api/v2/users

Header or media-type versioning communicates the version through an HTTP header or Accept media type.

Accept: application/vnd.example.v2+json

Versioning is important when introducing breaking changes such as changing response structures, removing fields, or altering endpoint behavior. It gives clients time to migrate and allows multiple API contracts to coexist during a transition.

title: What is the difference between localStorage, sessionStorage, and HttpOnly Cookies for storing tokens?
answer:
localStorage stores data persistently in the browser until it is explicitly removed. It is accessible to JavaScript, which means an XSS vulnerability can potentially expose tokens stored there.

sessionStorage is also accessible to JavaScript but is scoped to the browser tab/session and is generally cleared when the tab is closed.

HttpOnly Cookies cannot be read by JavaScript when the HttpOnly attribute is set. They are automatically sent with matching HTTP requests. Secure authentication cookies should generally also use Secure and an appropriate SameSite policy.

For authentication sessions, HttpOnly cookies are often preferred when the architecture supports cookie-based authentication because they reduce direct token exposure to JavaScript. Cookie-based authentication still requires appropriate CSRF protections.

title: How do Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) and Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) impact REST API integration, and how do you mitigate them?
answer:
XSS occurs when an attacker causes malicious script to execute in the context of a trusted website. If authentication tokens are accessible to JavaScript, XSS can potentially steal them.

Mitigations include output encoding, avoiding unsafe HTML injection, sanitizing untrusted HTML, using a strong Content Security Policy, and keeping sensitive tokens out of JavaScript-accessible storage when possible.

CSRF occurs when an attacker's site causes a victim's browser to send an authenticated request to another site, which is especially relevant when authentication relies on automatically attached cookies.

CSRF mitigations include SameSite cookies, anti-CSRF tokens, origin or referer validation where appropriate, and designing state-changing APIs with appropriate authentication and validation controls.

title: How does browser HTTP caching work using Cache-Control, ETag, and If-None-Match?
answer:
Cache-Control tells browsers and intermediary caches how a response can be stored and reused.

Cache-Control: max-age=3600, public

An ETag is a validator representing a particular version of a resource.

ETag: "abc123"

When the cached response becomes stale or requires validation, the browser can send:

If-None-Match: "abc123"

If the resource has not changed, the server can return 304 Not Modified, allowing the browser to reuse its cached representation instead of downloading the body again.

This reduces bandwidth while still allowing the client to validate whether cached content is current.

title: How do you implement client-side caching and optimistic UI updates for REST endpoints?
answer:
Client-side caching stores API responses locally so repeated requests can reuse existing data and reduce network traffic. Libraries such as TanStack Query provide caching, stale-time management, background refetching, invalidation, retries, and request deduplication.

Optimistic updates update the UI immediately based on the expected result of a mutation, before the server confirms it.

  1. Save the current cached data.
  2. Apply the expected change to the cache immediately.
  3. Send the mutation request.
  4. If it succeeds, reconcile the cache with the server response.
  5. If it fails, restore the previous cached data and show an error.

This creates a faster user experience while still providing a rollback path when the server rejects the mutation.

title: What is pagination in REST APIs (Cursor-based vs. Offset-based), and how do you implement infinite scroll on the front-end?
answer:
Offset-based pagination uses parameters such as page and limit, or offset and limit. It is simple but can become inefficient for large offsets and can produce duplicates or skipped records when data changes during pagination.

Cursor-based pagination uses a cursor representing a position in the dataset. The client sends a cursor such as after or nextCursor to request the next set of records. It is generally better suited to large or frequently changing datasets.

For infinite scroll, the front end can use IntersectionObserver to detect when a sentinel element near the bottom of the list becomes visible. It then requests the next page, appends the results to the existing list, and stops when the API indicates there are no more pages.

if (hasNextPage && !isFetching) {
  fetchNextPage(nextCursor);
}

Client-side caching libraries such as TanStack Query can simplify infinite queries, pagination state, request deduplication, and cache management.

title: What is GraphQL, and what core problems of REST such as Over-fetching and Under-fetching does it solve?
answer:
GraphQL is a strongly typed API query language and runtime that allows clients to request exactly the data they need.

It addresses common REST data-fetching problems:

  • Over-fetching: A REST endpoint may return more fields than the client needs. GraphQL allows the client to select only the required fields.
  • Under-fetching: A REST API may require multiple requests to retrieve related resources. GraphQL can combine related data into a single operation.

GraphQL also provides a strongly typed schema, introspection, reusable fragments, and a consistent query model for fetching related data.

title: What are the core components of a GraphQL service such as Schema, Types, Resolvers, Queries, Mutations, and Subscriptions?
answer:
• Schema: Defines the API contract, including available types, fields, arguments, and operations.
  • Types: Describe the shape of data, including scalars, objects, interfaces, unions, enums, and input objects.
  • Resolvers: Functions that provide the data for fields defined by the schema.
  • Queries: Read operations used to retrieve data.
  • Mutations: Operations used to modify server-side data.
  • Subscriptions: Operations that allow clients to receive ongoing real-time updates.

The schema defines what clients are allowed to request, while resolvers determine how the requested data is obtained.

title: What is the GraphQL Schema Definition Language (SDL), and what are Scalar vs. Object types?
answer:
GraphQL SDL is the language used to define a GraphQL schema. It describes types, fields, arguments, relationships, queries, mutations, subscriptions, directives, and other schema elements.

Scalar types represent leaf values such as String, Int, Float, Boolean, and ID. Custom scalars such as DateTime can also be defined.

Object types represent structured entities containing fields that can reference scalar values or other GraphQL types.

scalar DateTime

type User {
  id: ID!
  name: String!
  createdAt: DateTime!
}

title: Explain the difference between Queries, Mutations, and Subscriptions in GraphQL.
answer:
• Query: Used to read or retrieve data. Queries should generally be treated as read-only operations.
  • Mutation: Used to modify server-side state, such as creating, updating, or deleting records.
  • Subscription: Used for long-lived real-time communication where the server pushes relevant events to the client as they occur.
type Query {
  user(id: ID!): User
}

type Mutation {
  createUser(input: CreateUserInput!): User!
}

type Subscription {
  userUpdated: User!
}

title: What is the single HTTP endpoint model used by GraphQL, such as POST /graphql, and how does HTTP status code handling differ from REST?
answer:
GraphQL commonly exposes a single HTTP endpoint such as POST /graphql. The requested operation, fields, arguments, and variables are contained in the GraphQL request body rather than being represented by separate resource URLs.

GraphQL can return both data and an errors array in the same response. For example, a field can fail while other requested fields successfully return data.

Therefore, HTTP status codes alone do not always represent application-level success or failure in GraphQL in the same way they commonly do in REST. A successful HTTP response can contain GraphQL execution errors, so clients should inspect both the HTTP response and the GraphQL errors field.

title: How do you write a dynamic GraphQL query using variables and directives such as @include and @skip?
answer:
GraphQL variables allow clients to pass dynamic values into an operation without constructing query strings manually.

query GetUser($id: ID!, $includeEmail: Boolean!) {
  user(id: $id) {
    id
    name
    email @include(if: $includeEmail)
    phone @skip(if: $includeEmail)
  }
}

The variables can be supplied separately:

{
  "id": "123",
  "includeEmail": true
}

@include includes a field or fragment when its condition is true, while @skip excludes it when its condition is true.

title: What are GraphQL Fragments, and how do they promote component co-location and code reusability?
answer:
Fragments are reusable selections of fields that can be included in multiple GraphQL operations.

fragment UserCardFields on User {
  id
  name
  avatar
}

query GetUsers {
  users {
    ...UserCardFields
  }
}

In React applications, fragments can be colocated with the component that consumes the data. This makes the component's data requirements explicit and allows the same field selection to be reused across queries without duplicating field lists.

title: What are Inline Fragments and how are they used when querying Interfaces or Unions?
answer:
Inline fragments allow clients to request fields specific to a particular concrete type when a field returns an interface or union.

query Search {
  search(query: "react") {
    ... on User {
      id
      username
    }
    ... on Post {
      id
      title
    }
  }
}

Here, the ... on User fragment requests fields available only on User, while ... on Post requests fields available only on Post. This is particularly useful when a single field can return multiple object types.

title: How do GraphQL Subscriptions work under the hood using WebSockets?
answer:
A GraphQL subscription establishes a long-lived communication channel between the client and server. WebSockets are commonly used for this purpose, although other transport mechanisms can be implemented.

The client establishes the WebSocket connection and sends a subscription operation using a supported protocol such as graphql-ws. The server registers the subscription against an event or Pub/Sub source.

When a relevant event occurs, the server executes the subscription's selection set and sends the resulting payload through the active connection.

This is useful for real-time features such as notifications, chat, live dashboards, and collaborative applications.

title: Explain how pagination is implemented in GraphQL using the Relay Cursor Connections specification.
answer:
The Relay Cursor Connections pattern provides a standardized structure for cursor-based pagination. A connection commonly contains edges, nodes, and pageInfo.

query GetPosts {
  posts(first: 10, after: "cursor_xyz") {
    edges {
      cursor
      node {
        id
        title
      }
    }
    pageInfo {
      hasNextPage
      endCursor
    }
  }
}

The client uses first to specify how many records to retrieve and after to specify the cursor after which results should be returned. The endCursor can be used for the next request, while hasNextPage indicates whether more records are available.

title: What is Apollo Client or Urql, and what role does its normalized cache play?
answer:
Apollo Client and Urql are GraphQL client libraries for managing GraphQL operations, caching, loading states, errors, and application data.

A normalized cache stores entities independently using stable identifiers, often combining the type name and entity ID. Instead of storing complete nested query responses separately, multiple queries can reference the same cached entity.

When a normalized entity is updated, components or queries that depend on that entity can receive the updated value without requiring every complete query response to be stored or manually replaced.

title: How do you execute queries and mutations in React using Apollo hooks such as useQuery, useMutation, and useLazyQuery?
answer:
Apollo Client provides React Hooks for executing GraphQL operations.

useQuery executes a query when the component renders:

const { data, loading, error } = useQuery(GET_USERS);

useMutation returns a function that can be called when an action occurs:

const [createUser, { loading }] = useMutation(CREATE_USER);

await createUser({
  variables: { name: 'Mani' }
});

useLazyQuery returns a function that allows the query to be triggered manually, such as when a user clicks a button or submits a search form:

const [searchUsers, { data }] = useLazyQuery(SEARCH_USERS);

searchUsers({ variables: { query: 'react' } });

title: How do Optimistic UI updates work in GraphQL client libraries during mutations?
answer:
Optimistic UI allows the client to update the interface immediately using an expected mutation result rather than waiting for the server response.

For example, Apollo Client can receive an optimisticResponse that represents the expected successful result. The normalized cache is temporarily updated with that data, so the UI responds immediately.

When the real server response arrives, the client reconciles the optimistic result with the actual result. If the mutation fails, the optimistic changes are rolled back and the UI can display the error.

title: How do you handle cache updates manually after a mutation using cache.modify or refetchQueries?
answer:
After a mutation, the GraphQL client's cache may need to be updated so the UI reflects the new server state.

cache.modify allows Apollo Client to update specific fields in the normalized cache without fetching the entire query again. This is useful for adding or removing an item from a cached list.

cache.modify({
  fields: {
    todos(existingTodos = []) {
      return [...existingTodos, newTodoRef];
    }
  }
});

refetchQueries instructs Apollo Client to execute specific queries again after the mutation. It is simpler and can be useful when the affected cache relationships are complex, although it may result in additional network requests.

title: What is local state management in Apollo Client using Reactive Variables or the @client directive?
answer:
Apollo Client can manage application-local state alongside remote GraphQL data using mechanisms such as Reactive Variables and client-side cache fields.

A reactive variable can store a value outside React state while allowing Apollo queries and components that depend on it to react to changes.

const themeVar = makeVar('light');

themeVar('dark');

Historically, Apollo Client also supported the @client directive for explicitly marking fields as client-only. Modern Apollo applications commonly use cache fields and reactive variables for local state rather than relying on the older @client local-resolver model.

title: What is the N+1 Problem in GraphQL resolvers, and how is it resolved on the backend using DataLoader?
answer:
The N+1 problem occurs when a GraphQL query retrieves N parent records with one database query and then executes a separate database query for each parent's related data.

For example, retrieving 100 users and then loading each user's orders individually could result in 101 database queries.

DataLoader solves this by collecting multiple load requests during a request and batching them into a single operation:

const orders = await orderLoader.load(user.id);

The loader can combine many IDs into a query such as SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id IN (...). It also provides request-scoped caching so repeated requests for the same key can reuse the same result.

title: How does caching at the HTTP/CDN level differ between REST APIs and GraphQL APIs?
answer:
REST naturally maps resources to different URLs, making HTTP caching straightforward. A CDN can cache responses for URLs such as /api/products/123 according to HTTP cache headers.

GraphQL commonly uses a single endpoint such as /graphql, often with POST requests. Different queries and variables can produce different responses from the same URL, making conventional URL-based CDN caching more difficult.

GraphQL applications can improve HTTP caching through techniques such as persisted queries, GET requests for suitable operations, Cache-Control headers, and CDN-aware caching strategies. Client-side normalized caching is a separate layer and should not be confused with HTTP/CDN caching.

title: What are GraphQL Schema Directives, and how can they be used for authorization?
answer:
GraphQL Schema Directives attach metadata or behavior to schema definitions. Custom directives can be used to express application-specific policies declaratively.

For authorization, a schema might define a directive such as:

directive @auth(requires: Role!) on FIELD_DEFINITION

type Query {
  adminReport: Report @auth(requires: ADMIN)
}

The GraphQL server can implement the directive so that authentication or authorization is evaluated before the field resolver executes.

Authorization should still be enforced in the underlying business or service layer where necessary so that sensitive operations cannot be bypassed through another API path.

title: What is GraphQL Federation, and how does it allow multiple microservices to expose a single unified Graph?
answer:
GraphQL Federation allows multiple independently owned GraphQL services, called subgraphs, to contribute to a unified API.

Each subgraph owns part of the domain, such as Users, Products, or Orders. Federation directives define entities, keys, ownership, and relationships between domains.

A router receives the client's GraphQL operation, creates a query plan, sends the required sub-operations to the appropriate subgraphs, and combines their responses into a single GraphQL response.

This allows teams to develop and deploy domain services independently while clients interact with one unified graph.

title: How do you handle file uploads in GraphQL?
answer:
GraphQL's core specification does not define a native binary file-upload mechanism. Common approaches include multipart upload specifications and direct uploads to object storage.

With a GraphQL multipart request, a client sends the file as multipart/form-data and the server maps the uploaded file to a GraphQL operation.

A scalable alternative is to use a GraphQL mutation to generate a short-lived pre-signed upload URL. The client then uploads the binary file directly to object storage such as S3.

Direct-to-storage uploads are often preferable for large files because the GraphQL server does not need to proxy the entire binary payload.

title: How do you secure a GraphQL API against deeply nested malicious queries using Query Depth Limiting and Cost Analysis?
answer:
Query Depth Limiting analyzes the GraphQL AST and rejects queries that exceed a configured nesting depth. This helps prevent recursive structures such as user → friends → friends → friends from becoming excessively deep.

Query Cost Analysis assigns costs to fields and calculates an estimated total cost before execution. Expensive list fields can receive higher costs or multipliers based on their requested size.

Production GraphQL APIs can combine these protections with pagination limits, rate limiting, persisted queries, timeouts, authentication, and resource-level limits.

title: What is Schema Stitching vs. GraphQL Federation?
answer:
Schema Stitching combines multiple GraphQL schemas into a unified schema at a gateway or composition layer. The gateway can programmatically transform schemas and configure resolvers to connect related types.

GraphQL Federation uses a declarative specification in which subgraphs define their ownership, entities, keys, and relationships using federation directives. A federation router uses this information to compose the supergraph and create query plans.

Stitching traditionally involves more gateway-side composition and custom integration logic, while Federation moves domain ownership and relationships into the subgraph schema model.

title: What are @defer and @stream in GraphQL, and how do they enable progressive UI rendering?
answer:
@defer allows a non-critical part of a GraphQL query to be delivered later instead of blocking the initial response. The client can render the initial data first and progressively display the deferred portion when it arrives.

@stream allows items from a list field to be delivered incrementally as they become available instead of waiting for the entire list.

query ProductPage {
  product(id: "123") {
    name
    ...ProductReviews @defer
  }
}

fragment ProductReviews on Product {
  reviews {
    id
    text
  }
}

These incremental delivery techniques can improve perceived performance by allowing the UI to display immediately available content while slower data continues to arrive.

title: How do you handle error management in GraphQL with partial errors in the errors array alongside partial data?
answer:
GraphQL can return partial data together with an errors array when one or more fields fail during execution.

{
  "data": {
    "user": null,
    "products": [
      { "id": "1", "name": "Laptop" }
    ]
  },
  "errors": [
    {
      "message": "Not authorized",
      "path": ["user"],
      "extensions": {
        "code": "UNAUTHENTICATED"
      }
    }
  ]
}

The path property helps identify which field failed, while extensions can contain machine-readable application-specific error codes.

Clients should therefore handle both successful partial data and errors rather than assuming that a GraphQL response is either completely successful or completely failed.

title: When would you choose REST over GraphQL, and vice versa, for a modern web application?
answer:
Choose REST when the API is resource-oriented, has relatively simple data requirements, benefits heavily from conventional HTTP semantics and caching, or needs straightforward integration with many external consumers. REST is also often a good choice for simple CRUD APIs, webhooks, file transfers, and public APIs where HTTP tooling and conventions are important.

Choose GraphQL when clients have different data requirements, screens need data from multiple related domains, over-fetching and under-fetching are significant problems, or the application benefits from a strongly typed schema and flexible client-driven queries.

The choice is architectural rather than ideological. Many modern systems use both approaches, selecting REST or GraphQL based on the specific domain, performance requirements, caching model, team expertise, and consumer needs.

title: You are building a large enterprise dashboard where 15 different components need shared state (user permissions, cart data, theme, preferences). Using Context API causes whole-app re-renders on minor updates. How do you resolve this?
answer:
Root Cause: Updating a Context value causes all consuming components to re-render, even if they only need an unchanged property.

Solution:

  1. Split Contexts: Divide the monolith context into single-responsibility providers, such as UserContext and ThemeContext.
  2. Context Selectors / Atomic State: Use state-management libraries that support atomic selectors, such as Zustand, Jotai, or Redux Toolkit. Components subscribe only to specific slices.
  3. Custom Context + useSyncExternalStore: Extract state outside React's render tree into a pub/sub store and connect components via useSyncExternalStore for atomic re-renders without third-party dependencies.

title: Your company is migrating a legacy React codebase to a Micro-Frontend architecture using 5 Module Federation hosts. How do you handle shared React versions and global state?
answer:
Shared React Dependencies: Configure Module Federation shared options with singleton: true and strictVersion: true to enforce a single runtime instance of React and ReactDOM across host and remote applications.

Global State Sharing:

  • Avoid sharing a monolithic store across micro-frontends.
  • Use custom browser events or a lightweight Pub/Sub event bus via the window object for asynchronous cross-application communication.

title: A commerce app requires optimistic UI updates for Add to Cart and Favorite actions. If the API fails, the UI must revert instantly without causing a flash or jank. How do you implement this?
answer:
Implementation Strategy:

  1. Store the previous state in a local variable before updating state immediately.
  2. Update local state or the React Query cache optimistically.
  3. Trigger the asynchronous API call inside a try/catch block.
  4. On failure, catch the error, roll back to the stored snapshot, and trigger a non-blocking toast or error message.

Modern React Approach: Leverage React Query / TanStack Query using onMutate, onError, and onSettled, or React 19's useOptimistic hook to handle optimistic transitions natively.

title: A financial reporting dashboard receives hundreds of WebSocket updates per second. The application UI stutters and freezes. How do you re-architect data flow?
answer:
Root Cause: React cannot process 100+ render operations per second without dropping frames.

Solution:

  1. Debounce/Throttle State Updates: Buffer incoming WebSocket payloads in a non-react ref using useRef or a worker thread, and push state updates in batches every 100–300ms using requestAnimationFrame or setInterval.
  2. Offload Processing to Web Workers: Parse and aggregate heavy WebSocket JSON payloads off the main thread.
  3. Selective Rendering: Use Canvas/WebGL for heavy data visualization or virtualized DOM nodes for tables, such as react-window.

title: How do you design a robust Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) system in React where routes and individual actions (Buttons, Tabs) are conditionally exposed?
answer:
Architecture:

  • Central Authentication State: Maintain user, permissions, and roles centrally in an authentication state or Context.
  • Route Level: Wrap route definitions in a ProtectedRoute, such as ProtectedRoute role="MANAGER" or allowedRoles={["ADMIN"]}, which checks permissions before rendering or redirecting.
  • Component/Action Level: Create a reusable component such as <Can perform="users:delete"><DeleteButton /></Can> or a custom hook such as usePermission("users:delete") to expose fine-grained permissions.

title: When would you choose useReducer over useState or Redux Toolkit? Give a concrete scenario from your experience.
answer:
Scenario: A complex multi-step checkout form with delivery states and rollback capabilities.

Why useReducer: useState can create multiple independent state setters, which can make complex state transitions harder to manage. useReducer consolidates multi-field update logic into deterministic reducer actions such as SET_STEP, UPDATE_FIELD, and RESET_FORM.

Why not Redux Toolkit: If the state is transient and isolated strictly to the checkout route or component lifecycle, putting it in global Redux adds unnecessary global state complexity.

title: How do you handle deeply nested forms, such as dynamic surveys, with React Hook Form or Formik without causing performance degradation on every keystroke?
answer:
Optimization with React Hook Form: React Hook Form uses uncontrolled components under the hood with refs, which helps prevent top-level parent re-renders on every keystroke.

Nested Control: Use Controller or useFieldArray combined with isolated child components and React.memo so only the active typing field needs to re-render.

Validation: Perform schema validation using Zod or Yup on blur or on submit rather than on every onChange event.

title: How do you manage offline state and sync data when the client reconnects to the network in a Progressive Web App (PWA)?
answer:
Implementation:

  1. Monitor network status using navigator.onLine and online/offline event listeners.
  2. Queue offline user mutations in IndexedDB, using libraries such as Dexie.js or localForage.
  3. Register a Background Sync Service Worker using the sync event, or trigger a synchronization process when the connection is restored.
  4. Process queued requests sequentially using idempotent API calls and update the UI through React Query cache invalidation.

This approach allows users to continue working while offline and synchronizes pending mutations when connectivity becomes available again.

title: A list containing 10,000 complex cards slows down page scrolling and degrades browser memory. How do you optimize?
answer:
Virtualization: Implement DOM virtual windowing using libraries such as react-window or react-virtualized to render only the visible viewport nodes, approximately 10–20 items plus a small buffer.

CSS Containment: Apply CSS containment such as contain: content; or contain: strict; where appropriate to allow the browser to optimize layout and rendering.

DOM Node Simplification: Flatten unnecessarily nested component and DOM structures and use React.memo with an appropriate custom comparison where it provides a measurable benefit.

title: You wrapped a child component in React.memo, but it continues to re-render every time the parent component changes. What are the common causes and solutions?
answer:
Common Causes:

  1. Referential Equality Loss on Props: Passing inline functions, object literals, or array literals creates new references on every parent render. Examples include onClick={() => {}} and style={{ margin: 0 }}.
  2. Unmemoized Callbacks or Derived Values: Functions and objects passed as props are recreated on every render when they are not memoized appropriately.
  3. children Prop: Passing inline JSX as children creates new React element objects on each parent render, which can cause a memoized child to render again.

Solutions:

  • Wrap callbacks with useCallback when stable function identity is useful.
  • Wrap derived objects or arrays with useMemo when stable references are useful.
  • Pass primitive IDs or values where possible and let the child fetch or select the required state.

title: How do useTransition and useDeferredValue differ, and when would you use each in a React 18+ app?
answer:
useTransition:

  • When to use: You control the state update code and want to mark state updates as non-urgent and interruptible.
  • Scenario: Filtering a large dataset on a user tab click. startTransition(() => setTab("all-data")) keeps the main thread responsive while the filtering work is processed concurrently.

useDeferredValue:

  • When to use: You do not control the state source, such as props received from a third-party Hook or parent component.
  • Scenario: Passing a fast-changing text input prop to a heavily computed UI subtree. const deferredQuery = useDeferredValue(query) defers subtree re-renders until higher-priority renders finish.

title: You notice layout shift (CLS) when loading image galleries or async components. How do you eliminate visual flickers using Suspense and CSS?
answer:
Solutions:

  1. Reserve Space: Use CSS aspect-ratio: 16/9 or skeleton loaders with explicit height and width to prevent layout shifts when content arrives.
  2. React Suspense + Transitions: Wrap navigation transitions in startTransition so React can keep the current UI visible during the transition instead of immediately replacing it with a new loading state.
  3. useLayoutEffect / CSS content-visibility: Use useLayoutEffect to synchronously adjust measurement-dependent UI elements before browser paint, and use CSS content-visibility where appropriate to optimize rendering.

title: What is the React Fiber architecture? How does its two-phase rendering (Render Phase vs Commit Phase) impact code execution?
answer:
Fiber Architecture: React Fiber is a rewrite of React's core reconciliation engine that breaks rendering into incremental units of work called Fibers. This allows rendering work to be paused, aborted, or prioritized.

Render/Reconciliation Phase — Asynchronous & Interruptible:

  • React traverses Fiber nodes.
  • It runs functional component bodies.
  • It computes differences and builds a work-in-progress tree.
  • Side effects such as API calls and DOM mutations must not be executed directly during this phase because rendering can run multiple times or be discarded.

Commit Phase — Synchronous & Uninterruptible:

  • React applies updates to the actual DOM.
  • React executes lifecycle-related effects such as useLayoutEffect and useEffect.

title: How do you identify, profile, and fix memory leaks caused by React components in production?
answer:
Identification: Use the Chrome DevTools Memory tab, including Heap Snapshots and Allocation Timelines, or the React Profiler to identify detached DOM nodes or unmounted Fiber nodes retaining state.

Common Causes & Fixes:

  1. Uncleaned Side Effects: Event listeners such as window.addEventListener, timers such as setInterval, or WebSocket connections created inside useEffect without a cleanup function. Add appropriate cleanup logic in the effect's return function.
  2. Uncancelled Async Requests: API calls can continue after a component becomes irrelevant. Use AbortController inside useEffect to cancel requests during cleanup.
  3. Large Object Retention: Closures capturing large datasets or global caches can keep objects alive longer than necessary. Remove unnecessary references and ensure caches have appropriate lifetimes.

title: An API call succeeds, but the component throws an unhandled runtime JS error during rendering. How do you prevent the whole React app from crashing to a white screen?
answer:
Solution: Implement class-based Error Boundaries using getDerivedStateFromError and componentDidCatch.

Strategy:

  1. Global Error Boundary: Place an Error Boundary at the root level to handle critical rendering failures and provide a fallback UI.
  2. Local Error Boundaries: Wrap isolated feature widgets, such as a Sidebar or individual Widget, so a failure in one feature does not break the entire application.
  3. Error Reporting: Integrate error-reporting services such as Sentry or LogRocket inside componentDidCatch.
class WidgetErrorBoundary extends React.Component {
  state = { hasError: false };

  static getDerivedStateFromError(error) {
    return { hasError: true };
  }

  componentDidCatch(error, errorInfo) {
    logToService(error, errorInfo);
  }

  render() {
    if (this.state.hasError) return <Fallback />;
    return this.props.children;
  }
}

title: You encounter a race condition where fast sequential user input triggers multiple API requests, and an earlier out-of-order response overwrites newer data. How do you fix it?
answer:
Option 1: AbortController (Native): Pass an AbortSignal to fetch or Axios inside useEffect and invoke controller.abort() in the cleanup function.

Option 2: React Query: Use React Query's cancellation and request-management capabilities to prevent stale out-of-order responses from overwriting newer data.

Option 3: Boolean Flag: Maintain an isMounted or isCurrent local variable inside the effect and discard responses that are no longer current.

title: How do you handle Stale Closures inside useEffect or useCallback when accessing dynamic state variables inside async callbacks?
answer:
Problem: A closure captures variables from its lexical environment at creation time. If state changes, asynchronous callbacks or event handlers can execute with an old, stale state value.

Solutions:

  1. Functional State Updates: Replace setCount(count + 1) with setCount(prev => prev + 1) so the update receives the latest state.
  2. useRef Pattern: Store changing values inside a ref, such as ref.current = latestValue. Refs maintain a stable object across renders without causing re-renders when the current value changes.
  3. Correct Dependency Array: Ensure all state variables and values read by the effect or callback are correctly declared in its dependency array.

title: In React 18 StrictMode in development mode, useEffect fires twice on mount. This breaks an analytics tracking hook and doubles API calls. How do you handle this properly?
answer:
Explanation: React StrictMode deliberately mounts, unmounts, and remounts components in development to expose missing cleanup logic and help make components resilient to concurrent rendering behavior.

Correct Fix: Do not suppress StrictMode. Ensure effects have robust cleanup logic:

  • Cancel timers and remove event listeners.
  • Use AbortController for cancellable API requests.

For Strict Single Executions: For operations such as analytics tracking that intentionally need to happen only once per session, use an idempotent or once-per-session mechanism such as hasFiredRef.current, or track execution outside the React lifecycle in a global session store.

title: You receive a production error page: Infinite re-render loop detected / Maximum update depth exceeded. How do you systematically debug and locate the source?
answer:
Debugging Steps:

  1. Inspect the Stack Trace: Use the browser console or Error Boundary information to locate the component responsible for the repeated updates.
  2. Check State Updates During Rendering: Look for unintentional calls to setState() directly inside the component body instead of inside an event handler or appropriate effect.
  3. Check useEffect Dependencies: Look for functions or objects recreated on every render that are included in dependency arrays without appropriate stabilization using useMemo or useCallback.
  4. Use React DevTools Profiler: Enable the option to record why components rendered and identify the component repeatedly triggering updates.

title: Why can't you call Hooks conditionally inside if statements or loops, and how does React enforce this under the hood?
answer:
Under the Hood: React tracks Hooks for a component instance using an internal linked list or equivalent structure of memoized Hook state. React relies on the exact order of Hook calls across renders to associate each Hook call with its corresponding state or effect information.

Consequence of Conditional Hooks: Placing a Hook inside an if statement or loop can change the order or number of Hook calls when conditions change. This can corrupt the Hook state mapping and trigger React's Rules of Hooks errors.

Therefore, Hooks should always be called at the top level of React function components or custom Hooks, while conditional logic should be placed inside the Hook callback or around the rendered result rather than around the Hook call itself.

title: Design a production-grade custom useFetch hook that supports caching, automatic retry on failure, request deduplication, and cancellation on unmount.
answer:
The provided implementation uses React state, a ref-based cache, useCallback, AbortController, and retry logic to build a reusable data-fetching Hook.

import { useState, useEffect, useCallback, useRef } from 'react';

export function useFetch(url: string, retries = 3) {
  const [data, setData] = useState<T | null>(null);
  const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true);
  const [error, setError] = useState<Error | null>(null);
  const cache = useRef<Map<string, any>>(new Map());

  const fetchData = useCallback(async () => {
    if (cache.current.has(url)) {
      setData(cache.current.get(url));
      return;
    }

    setLoading(true);
    let attempt = 0;

    while (attempt < retries) {
      const controller = new AbortController();

      try {
        const res = await fetch(url, { signal: controller.signal });
        if (!res.ok) throw new Error(res.statusText);

        const json = await res.json();
        cache.current.set(url, json);
        setData(json);
        setError(null);
        break;
      } catch (err: any) {
        attempt++;
        if (attempt >= retries || err.name === 'AbortError') {
          setError(err);
        }
      } finally {
        setLoading(false);
      }
    }
  }, [url, retries]);

  useEffect(() => {
    fetchData();
  }, [fetchData]);

  return { data, loading, error, refetch: fetchData };
}

title: You need to create a modal/tooltip system that renders floating UI elements detached from parent DOM overflow constraints. How do you implement this using React Portals?
answer:
Implementation:

  1. Add a portal container such as <div id="portal-root"></div> to index.html.
  2. Create a Portal component using ReactDOM.createPortal(children, document.getElementById('portal-root')).
  3. Manage event bubbling carefully. Events inside a portal bubble through the React component tree rather than the physical DOM tree. Use e.stopPropagation() when parent React components should not receive the event.
function Portal({ children }) {
  const container = document.getElementById('portal-root');
  return ReactDOM.createPortal(children, container);
}

title: How do you design a Compound Component pattern in React, such as <Select.Option />, using Context API?
answer:
The Compound Component pattern allows related components such as Select and Select.Option to share state implicitly through Context while giving consumers a flexible and expressive API.

const SelectContext = createContext(null);

export function Select({ children, value }: any) {
  const [selectedOption, setSelectedOption] = useState(value);
  const select = (val: any) => setSelectedOption(val);

  return (
    <SelectContext.Provider value={{ selectedOption, select }}>
      {children}
    </SelectContext.Provider>
  );
}

Select.Option = function Option({ value, children }: any) {
  const { selectedOption, select } = useContext(SelectContext);

  return (
    <div
      className={`option ${selectedOption === value ? 'selected' : ''}`}
      onClick={() => select(value)}
    >
      {children}
    </div>
  );
};

title: How would you refactor legacy Class Components containing componentDidMount, componentDidUpdate, and componentWillUnmount to Modern Functional Hooks without introducing bug regressions?
answer:
The lifecycle logic can be mapped to functional Hooks while carefully preserving dependency and cleanup behavior.

  • componentDidMount: Use useEffect(() => { ... }, []).
  • componentDidUpdate: Use useEffect(() => { ... }, [dep1, dep2]), ensuring guard logic checks whether relevant values actually changed when necessary.
  • componentWillUnmount: Return a cleanup function from useEffect, such as useEffect(() => { return () => { ... } }).
  • this.state: Replace with useState or useReducer.
  • Class instance variables: Replace with useRef.

During migration, lifecycle side effects, cleanup behavior, dependency relationships, and state transitions should be preserved carefully to avoid behavioral regressions.

title: How do you build a custom useDebounce hook to delay execution of user input search?
answer:
A custom useDebounce Hook delays updating the returned value until the specified delay has elapsed without another value change. The existing timer is cleaned up whenever the value or delay changes.

function useDebounce(value: T, delay: number): T {
  const [debouncedValue, setDebouncedValue] = useState(value);

  useEffect(() => {
    const timer = setTimeout(() => {
      setDebouncedValue(value);
    }, delay);

    return () => clearTimeout(timer);
  }, [value, delay]);

  return debouncedValue;
}

This is useful for search inputs because the API request can use the debounced value instead of firing a request for every individual keystroke.

title: Explain Higher-Order Components (HOC) vs. Render Props vs. Custom Hooks. Which pattern is preferred today for cross-cutting concerns?
answer:
HOCs: A Higher-Order Component is a function that takes a component and returns an enhanced component. Drawbacks include wrapper hell, prop collisions, and implicit prop origins.

Render Props: A component receives a function prop that determines the rendered output dynamically. The main drawback is verbose JSX nesting.

Custom Hooks: Custom Hooks encapsulate reusable stateful logic without modifying the component hierarchy or adding wrapper components.

Verdict: Custom Hooks are generally preferred today for cross-cutting stateful logic. HOCs can still be useful for root-level component wrapping, such as withAuth or withTheme.

title: What is the difference between Server-Side Rendering (SSR), Static Site Generation (SSG), and React Server Components (RSC)? When would you use each?
answer:
SSR: Server-Side Rendering generates HTML per request at runtime on the server. It is suitable for dynamic or personalized content and data that needs to be generated for each request.

SSG: Static Site Generation generates HTML at build time. It is suitable for marketing websites, blogs, documentation, and other pages that can be generated ahead of time and heavily cached.

React Server Components (RSC): Server Components execute exclusively on the server and do not send their component JavaScript to the client. They can directly access server-side data sources and are useful for data fetching and heavy non-interactive rendering.

In the Next.js App Router, Server Components are the default component model, while Client Components are introduced where interactivity, state, effects, or browser APIs are required.

title: React and Next.js App Router Server Components (RSC): A developer adds useState to a Server Component, causing a build failure. How do you resolve this and architect Client/Server boundaries?
answer:
Fix: Add the "use client" directive at the top of the file that requires state, event listeners, or browser APIs.

"use client";

import { useState } from "react";

Architecture Strategy: Keep Server Components high in the component tree so they can perform server-side data fetching and access server resources directly. Push "use client" boundaries down toward leaf components such as buttons, forms, and interactive controls.

This approach minimizes the amount of JavaScript sent to the browser while keeping interactive functionality in Client Components.

title: Explain React DOM Hydration and the dreaded "Text content does not match server-rendered HTML" error. How do you prevent and resolve it?
answer:
Hydration is the process where client-side React attaches event handling and React behavior to HTML that was already rendered on the server.

A hydration mismatch occurs when the HTML produced during the server render differs from what React produces during the client's initial render.

Common Causes:

  1. Browser-only APIs used during the initial render, such as window.innerWidth or localStorage.
  2. Dynamic values such as Date.now() producing different results between server and client.
  3. Invalid or incorrectly nested HTML.

Fixes:

  • Use useEffect for client-specific logic that should run after the initial render.
  • Use dynamic imports with { ssr: false } for components that must only execute on the client.
  • Ensure the server and client produce the same initial markup.

title: How do React 18 / 19 Server-Driven Streams using renderToPipeableStream improve Time To First Byte (TTFB) and First Contentful Paint (FCP)?
answer:
