Traditional server rendering can wait for the entire rendering process and required data before sending the final HTML response. React streaming allows the server to send HTML incrementally over an HTTP connection using Node.js streams.

With renderToPipeableStream, the application can stream an initial HTML shell quickly while slower parts continue rendering. Slow sections can be placed behind Suspense boundaries, allowing available content to reach the browser without waiting for every data source.

This can improve TTFB and perceived FCP because users receive useful HTML earlier. As additional chunks become available, they are streamed to the browser and React can progressively hydrate the interactive portions.

title: How do you prevent Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) attacks in React applications when rendering user-submitted dynamic HTML?
answer:
Mechanism: React automatically escapes strings rendered through JSX expressions, which prevents standard script injection through normal JSX rendering.

Danger Zone: Using dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: userHTML }} bypasses React's default escaping behavior.

Fix: Sanitize raw HTML strings using security libraries such as DOMPurify or sanitize-html before rendering them. A strict Content Security Policy (CSP) should also be configured as an additional defense-in-depth measure.

title: How do you protect sensitive API keys and secrets in React frontends?
answer:
Core Rule: Frontend JavaScript bundles are publicly inspectable. Never store secret API keys, database passwords, payment secret credentials, or other server-side secrets in environment variables that are exposed to the client, such as variables prefixed with REACT_APP_ or NEXT_PUBLIC_.

Architecture: Route private requests through a Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) or server-side proxy layer, such as Next.js API routes or other server-side code. The private credentials remain on the server and are never included in the browser bundle.

title: Write a unit test using React Testing Library and Vitest/Jest for an asynchronous component that fetches user profiles on mount.
answer:
Use React Testing Library to render the component, verify the initial loading state, and wait for the asynchronously fetched user data to appear.

import { render, screen, waitFor } from '@testing-library/react';
import UserProfile from './UserProfile';

test('fetches and displays user data on success', async () => {
  const mockUser = { name: 'John Doe' };

  fetch = jest.fn().mockResolvedValueOnce({
    ok: true,
    json: async () => mockUser
  });

  render(<UserProfile />);

  expect(screen.getByText(/loading/i)).toBeInTheDocument();

  await waitFor(() => {
    expect(screen.getByText('John Doe')).toBeInTheDocument();
  });
});

title: What is the philosophical difference between React Testing Library (RTL) and Enzyme? Why did the industry transition?
answer:
Enzyme (Legacy): Focused heavily on implementation details, such as component state, internal class methods, and shallow component rendering.

React Testing Library (RTL): Focuses on testing component behavior from the end-user perspective. Tests interact with DOM elements and query accessible roles, text, and other user-visible behavior, such as getByRole('button').

Why the Transition: Tests based on implementation details could break when component internals were refactored even though the user-facing behavior remained unchanged. RTL tests are generally more resilient because they focus on observable behavior rather than internal implementation.

title: How do you configure Webpack/Vite for efficient code-splitting, tree-shaking, and minimal production bundle sizes?
answer:
Code Splitting: Use dynamic imports and React.lazy to split application code, commonly on a route-by-route basis.

const Module = React.lazy(() => import('./Module'));

Tree Shaking: Use ES module syntax with import and export so bundlers can statically analyze and remove unused code. For pure libraries, configure "sideEffects": false in package.json where appropriate.

Bundle Analysis: Use tools such as webpack-bundle-analyzer or rollup-plugin-visualizer to identify large dependencies. Replace unnecessarily large packages with smaller alternatives or import only the required modules. Webpack aliases can also help control which implementations are bundled when appropriate.

title: How do you implement robust internationalization (i18n) and localized dynamic imports in a global React application?
answer:
Use internationalization libraries such as react-i18next or FormatJS (react-intl) to manage translations and locale-aware content.

Dynamic Loading: Avoid bundling all locale translation JSON files into the main JavaScript bundle. Dynamically import the translation files based on the language selected by the user.

This reduces the initial bundle size and loads only the translations required for the current locale.

title: When should you use Controlled vs. Uncontrolled inputs? Describe a situation where Uncontrolled inputs are strictly required for performance.
answer:
Controlled: React state manages the input value on every keystroke using value={state} and onChange. This is useful for real-time field validation, dynamic form behavior, and enabling or disabling buttons based on input state.

Uncontrolled: The DOM manages the input value and React accesses it through a ref such as ref={inputRef}. This can be useful for text editors, search bars performing heavy real-time formatting, or dense tabular data input grids where triggering parent re-renders for every keystroke causes frame-rate drops.

Performance Scenario: Consider a large grid containing hundreds or thousands of inputs. Managing every input through top-level React state could cause expensive parent re-renders on every keystroke. Uncontrolled inputs can keep those updates closer to the DOM and reduce unnecessary React rendering.

title: How do you safely measure DOM element dimensions (height, width, offset) dynamically on screen resize?
answer:
Use the ResizeObserver API wrapped inside useLayoutEffect or a reusable custom Hook. ResizeObserver allows the application to react when the observed element's dimensions change.

function useComponentSize(ref) {
  const [size, setSize] = useState({ width: 0, height: 0 });

  useLayoutEffect(() => {
    if (!ref.current) return;

    const observer = new ResizeObserver((entry) => {
      setSize({
        width: entry.contentRect.width,
        height: entry.contentRect.height
      });
    });

    observer.observe(ref.current);

    return () => observer.disconnect();
  }, [ref]);

  return size;
}

The observer should always be disconnected during cleanup to prevent unnecessary observations after the component unmounts.

title: How do useRef and useState differ regarding component lifecycle renders?
answer:
useState: Updating state schedules a component re-render cycle and allows the updated value to be reflected in the UI.

useRef: Mutating ref.current is synchronous and does not trigger a React re-render. The ref object maintains its referential identity across renders.

Common use cases for useRef: Storing DOM elements, interval IDs, mutable values, or previous state values that need to persist between renders without causing another render.

title: What is Forwarding Refs (React.forwardRef) and when is it required?
answer:
Ref forwarding allows a parent component to pass a ref through a custom functional component to an underlying DOM element.

It is useful when a reusable component wraps a native element but the parent still needs imperative access to that underlying element, such as focusing an input.

Standard function components do not expose a ref to their internal DOM element automatically. React.forwardRef explicitly receives the ref and forwards it to the desired element.

const CustomInput = React.forwardRef((props, ref) => (
  <input
    ref={ref}
    className="input-style"
    {...props}
  />
));

title: How do React Query / TanStack Query manage cache invalidation, stale-while-revalidate state, and background sync?
answer:
Stale-While-Revalidate: React Query can return cached data immediately to the UI based on its configured staleTime, while a background refetch retrieves fresh server data. Once the request completes, the cache is updated and the UI reflects the latest data.

Cache Keys: Query keys identify cached data and act similarly to dependency identifiers, such as ['user', userId]. Calling queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['user'] }) marks matching cached queries as stale and can trigger a refetch for active queries according to the configured behavior.

title: How do you manage global modal dialog systems cleanly without cluttering component trees with isOpen states?
answer:
Pattern: Use a centralized Modal Provider with dynamic component rendering.

  1. Maintain a global modal stack array using Zustand or Context.
  2. Expose a global Hook such as useModal().openModal(ModalComponent, props).
  3. Render active modal components dynamically at the top level of the application.
  4. Use a React Portal to render the modal outside normal parent DOM constraints.

This keeps individual components from maintaining repetitive isOpen state and provides a consistent mechanism for opening, closing, and stacking dialogs.

title: How do you handle file uploads with progress bars, chunking, and cancellation support in React?
answer:
Progress Tracking: Use Axios with onUploadProgress or native XMLHttpRequest.upload.onprogress and store the current upload percentage in local React state.

Chunking: Slice large File objects into smaller chunks using file.slice(start, end). Upload the chunks sequentially or through a controlled concurrent queue.

const chunk = file.slice(start, end);

Cancellation: Connect an AbortController signal to the upload request and call controller.abort() when the user selects Cancel Upload.

For production-grade large-file uploads, the server should also track chunk identifiers and upload state so interrupted uploads can be resumed safely.

title: How do you approach Accessibility (a11y) in complex React components like Custom Comboboxes or Dropdowns?
answer:
Keyboard Navigation: Support keyboard interactions such as ArrowUp, ArrowDown, Enter, Escape, and Tab so users can operate the component without a mouse.

ARIA Attributes: Use appropriate semantics and attributes such as role="combobox", aria-expanded, aria-activedescendant, and aria-controls.

Focus Management: Manage focus programmatically with refs, for example ref.current.focus(), when opening, closing, or navigating the dropdown.

The component should also maintain a logical focus order and expose sufficient information to assistive technologies.

title: What is the difference between useLayoutEffect and useEffect? Give a concrete scenario where useEffect fails visual layout requirements.
answer:
useEffect: Runs after the browser has painted the updated UI. It is appropriate for most non-visual side effects such as subscriptions, data synchronization, and network operations.

useLayoutEffect: Runs synchronously after React has committed DOM mutations but before the browser paints. It is useful when code needs to measure or modify the DOM before the user sees the result.

Concrete Scenario: Consider measuring a DOM node's width to position a tooltip relative to an anchor button. If useEffect performs the measurement, the tooltip may initially render at the wrong position and visibly flicker before being corrected. useLayoutEffect can perform the measurement before paint, eliminating the visible positioning flicker.

title: How do you handle deep object state mutations cleanly without breaking React's immutability principles?
answer:
Standard React: Use nested spread operators to create new object references at every modified level.

setState(prev => ({
  ...prev,
  user: {
    ...prev.user,
    name: 'New'
  }
}));

Enterprise Solution: Use Immer, either through the use-immer Hook or Redux Toolkit's internal Immer integration. Immer uses ES6 Proxy objects to allow developers to write mutable-style updates against a draft while producing a new immutable state structure.

title: What is dynamic component loading, and how do you implement fallback loading boundaries with React.lazy and Suspense?
answer:
Dynamic component loading code-splits JavaScript bundles and fetches dynamic chunks on demand when the corresponding component needs to render.

React.lazy dynamically imports the component, while Suspense provides fallback UI while the chunk is loading.

const HeavyChart = React.lazy(() => import('./HeavyChart'));

function AnalyticsDashboard() {
  return (
    <Suspense fallback={<div>Loading chart...</div>}>
      <HeavyChart />
    </Suspense>
  );
}

title: How do you prevent memory leaks when establishing long-lived RxJS Observers or Event Emitters inside React components?
answer:
Subscribe to the observable or event emitter inside useEffect and strictly unsubscribe during the effect cleanup phase.

useEffect(() => {
  const subscription = dataStream$.subscribe((data) => {
    setData(data);
  });

  return () => {
    subscription.unsubscribe();
  };
}, []);

The cleanup function ensures that the subscription does not continue receiving events after the component unmounts, preventing unnecessary work and potential memory leaks.

title: How do you structure a production React application folder architecture for long-term scalability?
answer:
Use a Feature-First / Domain-Driven Architecture so feature-specific code remains colocated while shared infrastructure stays separate.

src/
├── features/
│   └── authentication/
│       ├── api/              # Feature-specific queries/mutations
│       ├── components/       # Isolated feature components
│       ├── hooks/            # Feature custom hooks
│       ├── types/            # Feature custom types
│       └── ...
├── components/               # Shared generic UI primitives
├── hooks/                    # Shared global utility hooks
├── store/                    # Global state stores
└── utils/                    # Helper functions and formatters

This structure keeps domain logic close to the feature that owns it while providing clear locations for reusable components, Hooks, global state, and utility functions.

title: How do React 19 Actions and the useActionState / useFormStatus hooks simplify server mutations and form state handling?
answer:
Actions: Allow asynchronous functions to be passed directly to form action props or used with action transitions, reducing the amount of manual mutation state management.

useActionState: Helps manage the result and pending state of an action, reducing the need to manually create separate useState values for form submission state, errors, and returned data.

useFormStatus: Allows child components inside a form to access the parent form's submission status. For example, a submit button can automatically disable itself while the form action is pending without requiring submission state to be passed through props.

title: What is the difference between UI and UX?
answer:
UI stands for User Interface. It focuses on the visual and interactive aspects of a product, such as colors, typography, buttons, spacing, and layouts.

UX stands for User Experience. It focuses on the overall experience of the user, including how easily they can complete their tasks, how intuitive the navigation is, and how efficiently the product solves their problem.

In simple terms, UI is about how the product looks and interacts, while UX is about how the user experiences the product.

Easy way to remember: UI = Look and Interaction. UX = Experience and Usability.

title: What is a user journey?
answer:
A user journey represents the complete experience a user goes through while interacting with a product to achieve a particular goal.

For example, in an e-commerce application, the journey could be discovering a product, searching, viewing the product details, adding it to the cart, checkout, payment, and finally receiving the order confirmation.

It helps us understand the user's goals, actions, touchpoints, pain points, and overall experience at each stage.

Key concept: Goal → Actions → Touchpoints → Pain Points → Outcome.

title: What is a user flow?
answer:
A user flow is the sequence of steps or screens a user follows to complete a specific task within an application.

For example, for an e-commerce checkout, the flow could be Cart → Address → Delivery → Payment → Order Confirmation.

User flow focuses more on the actual path and interactions required to complete a specific task.

Difference: A user journey represents the complete experience, while a user flow represents the specific path a user follows to accomplish a task.

title: What is a wireframe?
answer:
A wireframe is a low-fidelity representation of a webpage or application screen. It focuses mainly on structure, layout, content hierarchy, and functionality rather than colors and detailed visual design.

It helps product managers, UX designers, developers, and stakeholders agree on the structure before investing time in the final UI design.

In simple terms: A wireframe defines the structure and layout of a screen before detailed visual styling is added.

title: What is a design system?
answer:
A design system is a collection of reusable UI components, design guidelines, patterns, and design tokens that help teams build consistent digital products.

It can include typography, colors, spacing, buttons, inputs, cards, modals, accessibility guidelines, and interaction patterns.

From a frontend perspective, these design-system components can be implemented as reusable React components so that multiple applications maintain consistency and reduce development effort.

A strong way to explain it: A good design system creates a shared language between designers and developers.

title: What are Figma components and variants?
answer:
A Figma component is a reusable design element. For example, instead of designing every button separately, we can create one reusable Button component.

Variants allow us to define different states or properties of that component, such as primary, secondary, hover, disabled, or loading states.

For example, a Button component could have Primary, Secondary, Disabled, Hover, and Loading variants.

Figma components and React components follow a similar reusable-component concept, although they serve different purposes.

title: What is Auto Layout in Figma?
answer:
Auto Layout is a Figma feature that allows elements inside a frame to automatically adjust their position and size based on their content and layout rules.

It is useful for creating flexible and responsive designs, especially for buttons, cards, navigation bars, forms, and lists.

For example, if the text inside a button changes from Add to Cart to Add Product to Cart, Auto Layout can automatically adjust the button size based on the content.

Important concepts: Direction, Padding, Gap, Alignment, Hug Contents, Fill Container, and Fixed Width or Height.

title: How do you make a Figma design responsive?
answer:
First, I identify the responsive behavior defined by the design, such as breakpoints, container widths, spacing, typography, and component behavior.

In Figma, I would use Auto Layout, constraints, responsive components, and appropriate resizing rules.

During development, I would translate those rules into responsive CSS using Flexbox, Grid, media queries, fluid sizing, and responsive components.

Finally, I would validate the implementation against the Figma design at different viewport sizes, including desktop, tablet, and mobile.

Key concept: Figma constraints and responsive rules should translate into appropriate CSS layout and responsive behavior.

title: How do you convert Figma designs into React components?
answer:
I don't directly convert every Figma frame into an individual React component. First, I analyze the design and identify reusable patterns and components.

I identify design tokens such as colors, typography, spacing, border radius, and breakpoints. Then I create reusable components such as Button, Input, Card, Modal, Header, and Navigation.

After that, I compose these reusable components into page-level components and integrate the required API and state management.

Finally, I validate the implementation against the Figma design for responsiveness, accessibility, performance, and visual consistency.

Typical approach: Figma → Design Tokens → Reusable Components → Page Components → Business Logic → API and State Management → Responsive and Accessible UI.

title: How do you handle inconsistent designs from designers?
answer:
First, I identify whether the inconsistency is intentional or accidental.

If I find inconsistencies in spacing, typography, colors, or component behavior, I discuss them with the designer and product team rather than making assumptions.

If the same pattern appears across multiple screens, I recommend standardizing it through the design system.

My goal is to maintain consistency between the Figma design, design system, and actual implementation.

Strong approach: I don't blindly implement inconsistencies; I clarify them and try to establish a reusable pattern.

title: How do you improve the UX of an e-commerce checkout?
answer:
I would first analyze where users are dropping off in the checkout funnel.

Then I would simplify the checkout process by reducing unnecessary fields and steps, clearly displaying pricing and delivery information, providing inline validation, supporting guest checkout, and making payment options easy to understand.

I would also provide clear loading, error, and success states.

From a technical perspective, I would optimize performance because slow checkout experiences can directly affect conversion.

Finally, I would use analytics and A/B testing to validate whether the changes actually improve conversion.

Important UX principles: Fewer steps, guest checkout, clear pricing, no unexpected charges, inline validation, multiple payment options, mobile-friendly design, fast loading, clear error messages, and an always-visible order summary.

title: How do you design for accessibility?
answer:
I follow WCAG principles while designing and implementing the UI.

I consider sufficient color contrast, keyboard navigation, semantic HTML, proper labels for form fields, visible focus states, accessible error messages, alternative text for meaningful images, and appropriate ARIA attributes where necessary.

I also make sure the application works well with screen readers and different input methods.

I believe accessibility should be considered from the design stage rather than added at the end.

Four key WCAG principles: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, and Robust.

title: What makes a good form UX?
answer:
A good form should be simple, clear, and easy to complete.

I would use meaningful labels, logical grouping, appropriate input types, clear required-field indicators, inline validation, helpful error messages, and sensible tab order.

I would avoid asking for unnecessary information and preserve the user's entered data when validation fails.

On mobile, I would also use appropriate keyboard types and responsive layouts.

For example, instead of showing a generic message such as Invalid input, I would provide a specific message such as Please enter a valid email address, for example: name@example.com.

title: How do you handle loading, error, and empty states?
answer:
I treat loading, error, empty, and success states as part of the UX rather than edge cases.

During loading, I use skeletons or appropriate loading indicators depending on the context.

For errors, I provide a clear explanation of what happened and, when possible, a recovery action such as Retry.

For empty states, I explain why there is no data and provide a useful next action.

Example: For an order page that fails to load, I might display Unable to load your orders with a Try Again action. For an empty order history, I might display You don't have any orders yet with a Start Shopping action.

title: How do you improve a poor UI design?
answer:
First, I would understand the business goal and the user's problem before changing the UI.

Then I would evaluate the design based on usability, visual hierarchy, consistency, accessibility, responsiveness, and task completion.

I would identify the biggest usability problems and prioritize them rather than changing everything at once.

I would create alternative solutions, validate them with stakeholders or users, and use analytics or usability testing where possible.

Finally, I would implement the improvements through the design system and measure the impact.

My approach: Understand the Problem → Understand Users → Identify Pain Points → Prioritize Issues → Design Solutions → Prototype → Validate → Implement → Measure.

title: What is the difference between a low-fidelity and high-fidelity design?
answer:
A low-fidelity design is a simple representation of a product that focuses mainly on structure, layout, and user flow rather than detailed visual design.

A high-fidelity design is a detailed representation that includes colors, typography, images, spacing, components, interactions, and visual styling.

I would typically use low-fidelity designs during the early ideation and wireframing stage, and high-fidelity designs when the requirements and user experience have been validated.

In simple terms: Low fidelity focuses on structure and flow, while high fidelity focuses on the final visual and interactive experience.

title: What are design tokens?
answer:
Design tokens are reusable values that represent the fundamental visual properties of a design system.

They can include colors, typography, spacing, border radius, shadows, breakpoints, and other design values.

For example, instead of using different values for button colors throughout an application, we can define a common primary color token and reuse it across components.

From a frontend perspective, design tokens can be mapped to CSS variables or theme values so that the design system remains consistent between Figma and the application.

title: What is visual hierarchy in UI design?
answer:
Visual hierarchy is the way we organize and emphasize elements on a screen so that users can understand the importance and relationship of different pieces of information.

We can establish hierarchy using typography, font size, weight, color, spacing, alignment, contrast, and positioning.

For example, on a product page, the product name and price should generally receive more visual emphasis than secondary information such as product metadata.

A good visual hierarchy helps users scan the page quickly and understand what actions or information are most important.

title: What is mobile-first design?
answer:
Mobile-first design means designing and developing the experience for smaller screens first and then progressively enhancing it for larger screens.

I start by identifying the most important content and interactions that users need on mobile, where screen space is limited.

Then I expand the layout for tablet and desktop using responsive breakpoints, Flexbox, Grid, and responsive components.

This approach helps prioritize essential content, improve usability on smaller devices, and create a more scalable responsive design.

title: What is a design handoff from Figma to developers?
answer:
Design handoff is the process of transferring the design specifications and assets from the designer to the development team so that the UI can be implemented accurately.

During handoff, I review the Figma components, spacing, typography, colors, responsive behavior, interaction states, assets, and design tokens.

I also clarify any missing or ambiguous requirements with the designer before implementation.

As a frontend engineer, I focus on translating the design into reusable components rather than simply reproducing individual screens.

title: How do you ensure consistency between Figma and the React application?
answer:
I start by establishing a common design system between designers and developers, including colors, typography, spacing, components, and interaction patterns.

I map the Figma components and design tokens to reusable React components and CSS variables or theme values.

During implementation, I compare the application against the Figma design across different viewport sizes and states.

I also use code reviews and design reviews to identify inconsistencies and continuously improve the shared component library.

The goal is to maintain a single source of truth for reusable design patterns while keeping the design and implementation aligned.

title: How do you decide which elements should become reusable React components?
answer:
I look for elements that are repeated across multiple screens or have a clear, reusable behavior or visual pattern.

Examples include buttons, inputs, cards, modals, navigation, tables, dropdowns, and form controls.

I also consider whether creating a component will improve consistency, maintainability, testing, and accessibility.

I avoid creating components purely because an element appears once. The goal is to find the right level of abstraction without making the component overly complex.

My principle is: Reuse where there is a meaningful shared pattern, but avoid unnecessary abstraction.

title: How do you handle different UI states in a design?
answer:
I make sure the design considers all important states rather than only the default state.

Depending on the component, these can include default, hover, focus, active, disabled, loading, success, error, and empty states.

For example, a button may need normal, hover, focus, disabled, and loading states. A data table may need loading, populated, empty, and error states.

I ensure these states are visually clear, accessible, and consistent with the design system.

title: How do you improve the performance of a UI without affecting the user experience?
answer:
I first identify performance bottlenecks using tools such as Lighthouse, browser DevTools, and application performance monitoring.

Depending on the problem, I may use code splitting, lazy loading, image optimization, memoization, virtualization, bundle optimization, caching, and efficient API usage.

From a UX perspective, I also provide appropriate loading states and skeleton screens so that users understand what is happening.

My goal is not only to make the application technically faster but also to make the perceived experience faster and smoother for the user.

title: How do you collaborate with UX designers and product owners?
answer:
I collaborate with UX designers and product owners from the early stages rather than waiting until development starts.

I participate in requirement discussions, review user flows and Figma designs, identify technical constraints, and provide feedback on usability, accessibility, responsiveness, and feasibility.

If I find a potential issue in the design, I discuss it with the designer and product owner and propose alternative solutions based on technical and user requirements.

I also make sure the final implementation remains aligned with the approved design while maintaining scalability and maintainability.

As a technical lead, my goal is to create strong collaboration between product, UX, and engineering teams so that we solve the user's problem rather than simply implementing screens.
